description: When Malcolm Todd graduated high school in 2022, he told his parents he would be taking a gap year to pursue music. They, unsurprisingly, were less than thrilled by the proclamation, but gave him a year to see if it could work. They learned what the rest of the music industry quickly realized: never bet against Malcolm Todd. ?Every single day since I told my mom I wanted to do this, I have actively worked to grow my fanbase, to get better at music, to build this world,? he explains. By the time he shared Sweet Boy in 2024, his day job at Cold Stone was in the rearview. Tracks like ?Roommates? were racking up millions of streams daily. Fast forward a year, and Todd is more motivated than ever on his self-titled album, a declaration that he isn?t a hype machine or a flash in the pan, but a generation-defining voice.

The hair products may have changed, but the drama, the rivalries, and the thirst for hallway clout remain timeless. It is the musical you know and love, but dragged through a cloud of strawberry scented vapor and a TikTok filter. It's the show that you want (Ooh! Ooh! Ooh, honey!) Don't miss the Chicago premiere of this hit musical, straight from NYC. GREASE is no longer the word. Now the word is VAPE! - New York Post A must-see! A fun, irreverent night out. I couldn't stop laughing. - Hollywood Press Corps VAPE! is the one that you want! Clever, goofy and camp. - Theater Pizzazz Brash, fast and unapologetically smart. - Theaterscene.net VAPE! description: Sweet Pill has partnered with PLUS1 so that $1 from every ticket sold goes to Calling All Crows and their work mobilizing music fans and artists to fuel feminist movements. In addition to this partnership, Calling All Crows will also be providing the band with Mental Wellness Allyship Training focused on recognizing and responding to challenges on the road, helping equip them with tools and shared protocols to better support one another throughout the tour. Sweet Pill's sophomore album, Still There's a Glow, is a hard-fought document of self-reflection and growth. It is raw and real, stacked with a lyrical honesty that's matched by singer Zayna Youssef's soaring, expressive vocals. Written and recorded in the wake of a whirlwind three years following their 2022 debut LP, Where the Heart Is--and after scrapping essentially an entire album's worth of demos--Still There's a Glow is a dynamic, cathartic journey of making conscious change within oneself. , "rdquo" -> I went through some depression last spring, and then I went into therapy. It was also a big turning point in my life as I was about to turn 30, while I'd written our first record when I was graduating from college--that's a big change," Youssef explains. , "rdquo" -> I could've kept making bad choices because they're easy, but I had to come clean to myself. Half the album was written before and the other half after, so the songs are kind of hard on myself but some are also hopeful, with a light at the end of the tunnel. You put out a fire, there's still an ember that's still glowing--that's the record. It's about being at a low and climbing out of it." The close-knit New Jersey/Philadelphia quintet had been going virtually nonstop since the release of Where the Heart Is (Topshelf). They went on tour with bands including La Dispute and The Wonder Years, embarked on their own headlining runs--organically growing a devoted fanbase with their passionate live show, which Stereogum has lauded as , "rdquo" -> an immensely charming powerhouse...songs that obliterate the distinctions between power and finesse, between pop and hardcore, between emo and the larger continuum of crowd-pleasing rock 'n' roll." The young band earned co-signs from stars like Hayley Williams and Doja Cat, while continuing to tour nonstop worldwide and play festivals like Best Friends Forever, Riot Fest, and Outbreak. Though they were writing all the while, the exhaustion of new expectations and such an intense touring regimen took its toll. When the time came for Sweet Pill to begin recording the material they felt was meant to be their next album, Youssef was still figuring out what and how she wanted to sing on nearly half the songs. She was blocked--no matter how many times she sat down and tried, things wouldn't click into place. , "rdquo" -> I had just been trying to write these same parts for such a long time," she says. , "rdquo" -> You do it, you say it, and you don't even have to think about it really. You just make the sounds, noises, and words, and you think 'absolutely yes,' [but] it was like 'fuck, no' every single time. I couldn't differentiate between what was just being hard on myself, or if it was like actually 'fuck, no.' Now, I realize it was definitely 50/50." The band decided to start fresh and step away from most of the demos they'd created, choosing to instead pause, look inward, and move on their own time in order to ease the pressure they had been heaping on themselves over the past three years.

title: Shaping a Library | Exhibition
description: In early 1970, a San Diego newspaper announced, “Unique Library Taking Shape.” The headline referred to UC San Diego’s Central University Library, now Geisel Library, which was then under construction. The Library’s story began several years earlier. In 1965, architect William L. Pereira was invited to design the Central University Library, envisioned as the flagship building for the UC San Diego campus. Construction began in 1968, and by September 1971, the new Central University Library was dedicated. Over the decades, the building has continued to evolve through expansions and renovations, adapting to the changing needs of the campus community. Tracing the history of the Library’s site design process, construction and expansion from 1965 to 1993, Shaping a Library draws on unique materials from UC San Diego Library’s Special Collections & Archives. From Pereira’s original spherical concept for Geisel Library to Gunnar Birkerts’ glass-walled expansion, architectural drawings, photographs and documents reveal the ideas, people and processes that shaped this beloved campus landmark. Shaping a Library is on view in the Exhibition Gallery on the 2nd (main) Floor of Geisel Library during the building's open hours from Saturday, September 26 through Tuesday, December 8, 2026. Can’t make it to campus to view the exhibition in-person? View the digital exhibit. Image Credit: Architectural rendering of UC San Diego Central University Library, William L. Pereira and Associates, 1965. UC San Diego Library, Special Collections & Archives.

This exhibition presents selected works from the 2025 and 2026 issues, offering a glimpse into the experiences, perspectives and creative lives of the School of Medicine community. Visitors are invited to pause, reflect and explore the many dimensions of the human experience. The Human Condition: An Exploration of Art & Literature is on view in the Sally T. WongAvery Library breezeway from September 26 to December 13, 2026, during the building's open hours. Previous issues of The Human Condition magazine, dating back to 2007-08, are available to download and read at your leisure. title: Library Milestones | Exhibit
description: Before the rise of digital publications and licensed electronic resources, academic libraries measured the size of their collections by the number of physical volumes on their shelves. Reaching a million-volume milestone was a source of pride and a mark of growth. Together, they also reflect the generosity of donors and support groups who helped build the collections and offer a glimpse into what made a book milestone-worthy at the time. Library Milestones is on view outside of Special Collections & Archives on the 2nd (main) Floor of Geisel Library during the building's open hours through Sunday, December 13, 2026. Photo citation: John Ogilby. America: being the latest, and most accurate description of the New World; containing the original inhabitants, and the remarkable voyages thither... title: Commercialization Clinic
description: Commercialization Clinic Are you a builder, researcher, and founder who is ready to think seriously about commercialization, but not sure where to start? The Commercialization Clinic is an open, conversational space hosted by Anthony Reza Razavi once a month to drop in and explore the questions that matter most: When is the right time to file for IP protection?How does publishing impact my ability to secure IP protection?How do I bridge the gap between lab proof-of-concept and industry-ready prototype?How can I clearly differentiate my solution from existing alternatives?What types of partnerships could accelerate commercialization?How do I decide between licensing my technology to an existing company vs. forming a startup?How do I know if I’m “investor-ready”?What milestones make a technology attractive for licensing or acquisition?Surrounded by a curated collection of standout patents—hand-selected by the university's own commercialization team—you’ll be immersed in real examples of ideas that made the leap from concept to impact. What to Expect This isn’t a lecture. It’s a working session. Bring your ideas, early-stage inventions, or half-formed questions. Whether you're refining a disclosure, exploring startup pathways, or simply trying to understand how intellectual property fits into your work, this monthly clinic was designed to help you on your startup journey. You’ll walk away with: Clearer next steps on patents and IP strategyInsight into how commercialization actually unfoldsPractical guidance grounded in real industry and academic experienceMeet Your Host At the intersection of discovery and deployment, Anthony Reza Razavi leads the Life Sciences Innovation team at UC San Diego, bringing a rare combination of scientific expertise and commercialization experience. He has a diverse background as a scientist, business development and operations professional in pharmaceutical industry, startups and as a tech transfer and corporate partnership professional in academia. He worked previously at the Foundation Venture Capital Group, where he gained experience in the investment and management of Startups in the Life Sciences. Clinic Details The Commercialization Clinic hosted by Anthony Reza Rezavi at the Patent Studio is open once a month for the following office hours: WHEN: Second Thursday of the Month | 3-5 p.m. WHERE: Design & Innovation Building, Patent Studio, Room 451 No appointments necesary. Drop-ins welcome! What is the Patent Studio? Located in the Entrepreneurship Center in Room 451, the Patent Studio is a curated environment built to inspire commercialization thinking. The patents on display there aren’t random; they’re selected to spark ideas, challenge assumptions, and show what’s possible when innovation is protected and positioned effectively. Discover what intellectual property looks like up close. Hours are limited, so please first check with Anthony Reza Rezavi before stopping by.

title: SYML - Solo in North America 2026 with Roger Weeks
description: SYML is the solo venture of Seattle artist Brian Fennell. Welsh for , "rdquo" -> simple"--- he makes music that taps into the instincts that drive us to places of sanctuary, whether that be a place or a person. Fennell's latest offering, Nobody Lives Here, marks his clearest, crispest writing. Written, recorded, and produced by him and his longtime collaborator Brian Eichelberger, it is fueled by the keen understanding that life is a contradiction, a fleeting moment. But as we accept the presence of loss, we can still welcome others into our space with melody, lyrics, a slide guitar, or a cello's hum. His sense of humanity is his musical compass. As an artist, Fennell takes license to both gut and be gutted. , "rdquo" -> If the dark inspires the good, that's a good thing to be honest about," he says. He released his self-titled debut album in 2019, which includes the multi-platinum song , "rdquo" -> Where's My Love" and the Gold Record fan favorite , "rdquo" -> Girl." His 2023 sophomore album, The Day My Father Died, described by NPR as , "rdquo" -> euphoric," was recorded at Studio X with renowned producer Phil Ek and features collaborations with Elbow's Guy Garvey, Lucius, Sara Watkins of Nickel Creek, and Charlotte Lawrence. His music has become the soundtrack to countless films and TV shows and was used by Lana Del Rey on the song , "rdquo" -> Paris, TX," from her Grammy-nominated 2023 album. With over four billion streams, the multi-platinum artist looks at grief, loss, mortality, and the passing of time directly in the eye, unwavering and harmonious. In 2024, SYML launched the imprint, FIN. Recordings, a collaboration with his label, Nettwerk Music Group, and management Good Harbor Music.

description: Do you have old magazines, vintage zines, or leftover craft supplies? We are gathering materials for a community Collage Poetry project that will be turned into a public exhibition. Collage Poetry weaves together existing text and visual fragments such as magazine cutouts, newspaper snippets, book jackets, zines, school reports/papers, and even non-paper materials (yarn, ribbon, glitter) to form a new, layered work of art. Check out examples from the Alice Notley Artworks collection, like Alone - I Pour a Cup or Vacuum. What to Donate: We are seeking materials in any language, including: Magazines and newspapersBook jackets and zinesOld school reports or papersMixed media (yarn, ribbon, fabric scraps, etc.)Where to Donate: Donations can be dropped off at the collection boxes located in the Service Hubs at Geisel Library and WongAvery Library during each building’s open hours. View Geisel’s hoursView WongAvery’s hours (note: WongAvery is closed on Saturdays)Note: All donations are final and will not be returned. Please ensure all donated papers, reports, or documents are free of sensitive or personal information. We kindly ask that all donations be clean and free of mold, odors, or pests. For safety reasons, please do not donate hazardous materials, including broken glass, chemicals, or sharp metal objects. Questions? Contact us at ucsdlibrary@ucsd.edu.

title: Shaping a Library | Exhibition
description: In early 1970, a San Diego newspaper announced, “Unique Library Taking Shape.” The headline referred to UC San Diego’s Central University Library, now Geisel Library, which was then under construction. The Library’s story began several years earlier. In 1965, architect William L. Pereira was invited to design the Central University Library, envisioned as the flagship building for the UC San Diego campus. Construction began in 1968, and by September 1971, the new Central University Library was dedicated. Over the decades, the building has continued to evolve through expansions and renovations, adapting to the changing needs of the campus community. Tracing the history of the Library’s site design process, construction and expansion from 1965 to 1993, Shaping a Library draws on unique materials from UC San Diego Library’s Special Collections & Archives. From Pereira’s original spherical concept for Geisel Library to Gunnar Birkerts’ glass-walled expansion, architectural drawings, photographs and documents reveal the ideas, people and processes that shaped this beloved campus landmark. Shaping a Library is on view in the Exhibition Gallery on the 2nd (main) Floor of Geisel Library during the building's open hours from Saturday, September 26 through Tuesday, December 8, 2026. Can’t make it to campus to view the exhibition in-person? View the digital exhibit. Image Credit: Architectural rendering of UC San Diego Central University Library, William L. Pereira and Associates, 1965. UC San Diego Library, Special Collections & Archives.

title: The Human Condition: An Exploration of Art & Literature | Exhibit
description: The Human Condition: An Exploration of Art & Literature is an annual art and literary magazine created by medical students for the UC San Diego School of Medicine community. Now in its 32nd year, the student-led publication features art, photography, poetry, prose, sculpture, comics and more, providing a space for safe expression, creativity and exploring identities beyond medicine. This exhibition presents selected works from the 2025 and 2026 issues, offering a glimpse into the experiences, perspectives and creative lives of the School of Medicine community. Visitors are invited to pause, reflect and explore the many dimensions of the human experience. The Human Condition: An Exploration of Art & Literature is on view in the Sally T. WongAvery Library breezeway from September 26 to December 13, 2026, during the building's open hours. Previous issues of The Human Condition magazine, dating back to 2007-08, are available to download and read at your leisure. Curated by: Amy Xue, MS4, editor-in-chief, 2026-27 Myat Wai, MS4, editor-in-chief, 2026-27Supported by: UC San Diego School of MedicineUC San Diego Library

title: Library Milestones | Exhibit
description: Before the rise of digital publications and licensed electronic resources, academic libraries measured the size of their collections by the number of physical volumes on their shelves. Reaching a million-volume milestone was a source of pride and a mark of growth. This exhibit highlights five titles that mark milestones in the growth of the UC San Diego Library’s physical collections. Together, they also reflect the generosity of donors and support groups who helped build the collections and offer a glimpse into what made a book milestone-worthy at the time. Library Milestones is on view outside of Special Collections & Archives on the 2nd (main) Floor of Geisel Library during the building's open hours through Sunday, December 13, 2026. Photo citation: John Ogilby. America: being the latest, and most accurate description of the New World; containing the original inhabitants, and the remarkable voyages thither... London: printed by the author, 1671. UC San Diego Library, Special Collections & Archives.

title: Art Break
description: To Catch a Fish in 21st century contemporary culture is pretty easy, as mermaids are everywhere these days. From literature to film, art to advertising, mermaid museums to mermaid conferences (mercons), mermaids are surfacing and demanding attention. Today’s mermaids defy expectations of alabaster skin and blond hair, Christian ideals of female sexuality, and other genre conventions solidified in the wake of Hans Christen Andersen’s The Little Mermaid (1837) and Disney’s famous animated adaptation of it (1989). Today’s mermaids are Black and Brown, sexually fluid, and grounded in indigeneity. They rage against human destruction of the oceans and global capitalism but are also very much part of the contemporary culture industry— from mermaid kitsch to “MermaidCore” fashion. Hosted by Dr. Jessica Pressman, Professor of English and Comparative Literature at San Diego State University and mermaid scholar, this talk considers what we can learn by taking seriously the contemporary mermaid renaissance, catching a fish or two and carefully examining these examples as a means of understanding the larger current. What might mermaids—from contemporary culture AND Mingei’s exhibition—tell us about culture’s most pressing anxieties and concerns, past and present? Jessica Pressman is Professor of English and Comparative Literature at San Diego State University, where she co-founded SDSU’s Digital Humanities Initiative. She is the author of Bookishness: Loving Books in a Digital Age (Columbia University Press, 2020), Digital Modernism: Making It New in New Media (Oxford University Press, 2014), and co-author,_ with Mark C. Marino and Jeremy Douglass, of Reading Project: A Collaborative Analysis of William Poundstone’s Project for Tachistoscope {Bottomless Pit} (University of Iowa Press, 2015). She co-edited two volumes: Comparative Textual Media: Transforming the Humanities in the Postprint Era (University of Minnesota Press, 2013) with N. Katherine Hayles and Book Presence in a Digital Age _ (Bloomsbury Press, 2018) with Kiene Brillenburg Wurth and Kári Driscoll. She is at work on a book about 21st-century mermaid narrative. Her full CV can be found at www.jessicapressman.com. Image credit: Rosendo Rodriguez, Mermaid , 20th century, Mexico. Painted clay. 10 1/2 in. x 14 in. x 5 in. Gift of Mayde Meiers Herberg, 1999-02-002. Contact Shannon Foley

description: Inspired by the traditional fishing nets and nautical knots featured in To Catch a Fish , our newest Together workshop series, Knot Together , explores the art of macramé. The series is led by Sitoë Thiam, a fiber artist and mechanical engineer who bridges technical precision with organic expression. As the founder of Unknot, a design studio specializing in knotting and weaving, she brings a unique interdisciplinary perspective to the world of fiber arts. Knotted Treasure Pendant | Friday, October 9 | 5-7pm In October, discover the art of the miniature! Participants will transform small, personal talismans like river stones, sea glass, or cherished keepsakes into delicate, wearable sculptures. By mastering the rhythmic craft of the micro-net, you will learn to encapsulate these treasures in a custom mesh by adjusting density and form to suit each unique object. Whether finished with a strand of beads or left in its purest corded form, your creation becomes a portable piece of folk art. The Together series at Mingei invites makers of all skill levels to come together and create in a supportive, low-pressure environment. Past iterations— Sew Together, Weave Together , Dye Together , Stitch Together , and Clay Together —explore a variety of craft techniques while emphasizing collaboration, experimentation, and hands-on learning. Each workshop encourages participants to connect with materials, try new skills, and enjoy the process of making together.

description: MUNA?s journey has always been about bringing to light the complex, messy, ecstatic realities of life, and with their fourth album, Dancing On The Wall, they?ve never been sharper, darker, or more exhilarating. Emerging from the sparkly, confetti-strewn heights of their 2022 self-titled record, MUNA now channel the raw, anxious, and sweat-soaked energy of living in a city (Los Angeles) of unrelenting heat, a corrupted world wrought by political tension, and the quieter and more personal pressures of millennial precarity and heartache in these uncertain times. The result is a record that feels both intimate and spectacular: a fast-paced, hard-edged dance pop world built with teeth, wit, and emotional resonance?a soundtrack for hearts on fire amidst the tumult of modern life. Davy Knowles
description: Whether playing acoustic, mandolin, national steel, or screaming electric guitar, Davy Knowles has an unmistakable style.Since bursting on to the scene with his band Back Door Slams critically acclaimed album Roll Away in 2007 (I heard the spirit of Jimi Hendrix Patrick McDonald - Seattle Times), Davys star has only risen. His sophomore release Coming Up For Air was produced by the legendary Peter Frampton (Davy already has a recognizable style. Hes definitely the gunslinger guitarist of the 21st century,- Peter Frampton), with subsequent tours seeing him supporting and sharing the stage with acts such as Jeff Beck, The Who, Joe Bonamassa, Kid Rock, Lynyrd Skynyrd, George Thorogood, Brian Setzer, the Sammy Hagarfronted supergroup Chickenfoot, and guitar hero Joe Satriani who called Davy My favorite modern Bluesman. Knowles has several top-5 Billboard Blues charting albums under his belt, high profile TV appearances (Jimmy Kimmel Live and CBS Good Morning America among others), and has been praised with high accolades from heroes and press alike - but its not just the music industry who has taken note. Knowles was also the very first artist in history to perform live to the International Space Station directly from mission control in Houston TX, and has had his music taken to the Space Station by two astronauts, Nicole Stott and Ron Garan, on their respective missions orbiting Earth.Never one to be satisfied or to sit still, Knowles has explored multiple genres and styles, from the hard-hitting 70s classic rock influenced album Three Miles From Avalon, to the haunting acoustic delta blues of 1932, and the sweet, soul-searching folk of 2023s If I Should Wander. Whether spending an evening onstage armed with just an acoustic guitar, or wielding his well worn and trusty Telecaster while fronting his blues/rock trio - and at any point in between the two - Davy Knowles is one of the most versatile and formidable songwriters, vocalists and musicians in the world today. A true artist in every sense of the word.

title: Hank Ruff
description: As a recent graduate from Indiana University, Hank Ruff has been building a name for himself throughout the state of Indiana while being in college. After his latest EP ""Hellbender"" went #1 on the iTunes all-genre chart, Ruff hopes to further this momentum by beginning to play all over the midwest and beyond. Now that he is finished with school and pursuing music full-time, Ruff has dreams to bring his more neo-traditional brand of country music all over the country. Hank was born and raised in Southern Indiana, and has been playing country music around the state since the age of 11. Named after Hank Williams Sr., Ruff began playing the mandolin and playing at bluegrass jams, and eventually picking up the guitar and learning classic country songs like ""Hey Good Lookin"" and ""Mama Tried"". Ruff started playing with his dad's band, ""The Dew Daddies"", and soon after that he began writing songs with his dad by the time he was in high school. Most of Ruff's catalogue is comprised of songs that the two wrote together, including ""If the Boot Fits"". Filled with steel guitar and fiddle, these songs embody what Ruff and his music is all about: combining elements of the traditional country sound with modern influences, and bringing a little more of the classic elements of the distinctive country sound back into mainstream country music."

title: The Dead Bolts with Cab Ellis
description: The Dead Bolts. A true Rock band of the Modern Age, hailing from Chicago, IL. The Dead Bolts didn't come up through the industry - they earned every room they walked into. Eddie Hennessy, John Rolence, James Ryan, Matt Paske, Tyler Hancock, and Pat Corbett - six guys from the South Side who built the kind of band that feels less like a music project and more like a crew you want to be around. Their live show reflects exactly that. The kind of music that evokes Fontaines D.C., Local Natives, and early Kings of Leon. They've sold out rooms across Chicago, played Thalia Hall and Metro, and toured the entire country crammed in an SUV named Vancis with no crew and no safety net. Just a relentless belief in what they're doing. Now with their third record on the way and the momentum of Beau Monde still carrying, The Dead Bolts are stepping into a bigger moment with everything that got them here still fully intact. Raw, loud, and absolutely worth the drive.

title: Jahnavi Harrison
description: Jahnavi Harrison is a musician, writer, artist and practitioner of bhakti - yoga. She spent her formative years at Bhaktivedanta Manor in England, in a rich environment where mantra chanting and sacred art were a part of every day life. With a background in Western and Eastern classical music and dance, she has tried to pursue a path of self realisation and service through artistic expression. For nearly 20 years she has offered her voice and violin playing in the performance of original spiritual music and mantra kirtan, in diverse venues all over the world. She aspires to create art and facilitate experiences which heal, uplift and nourish the spirit. Now based in California; she regularly leads live gatherings, sound bath experiences, concerts and retreat s. Over the years Jahnavi has collaborated regularly with artists such as Deva Premal and Miten, Jai Uttal, Krishna Das, Snatam Kaur, Gaura Vani, and most recently, with Willow Smith with the EP Rise (2020). title: Tito Nieves - 50 Años La Historia Continua
description: Tito Nieves, born Humberto Nieves on June 4, 1958, in Río Piedras, Puerto Rico, is known as the "Pavarotti of Salsa" for his clear and powerful voice. Moving to New York City as a child, he grew up in a family of musicians & began his professional career in 1975 with Orquesta Cimarrón. He later worked with Héctor Lavoe, debuted with Johnny Ortiz's Taibori in 1978, and co-founded Conjunto Clásico, recording eight albums with the group before launching his solo career. His solo debut Classic (1988) went gold, followed by Yo Quiero Cantar (1989), which also went gold and featured the groundbreaking English-language salsa hit "I'll Always Love You." His 1990 album Déjame Vivir achieved platinum status, and I Like It Like That (1997), an all-English salsa album, brought mainstream exposure, including a performance with Stevie Wonder at the Alma Awards. Tito's later albums, including Dale Cara a la Vida (1998) and Clase Aparte (1999), showcase his blend of salsa, pop, and R&B influences.

title: ROBERT ELLIS Band at FITZGERALDS w/ special guest Philip Bowen
description: FITZGERALDS NIGHTCLUB PRESENTS: Robert Ellis at FITZGERALDS Nightclub w/ special guest Philip Bowen $25 General Admission / Reserved Tables Available Recorded live to tape in just two days, Robert Ellis's exquisite new album, Yesterday's News, is as stripped-down as it gets, with the celebrated songwriter and producer's delicate, reedy tenor accompanied only by nylon string guitar, upright bass, and the occasional piece of handheld percussion. The arrangements are harmonically sophisticated here, drawing on the open tunings and intricate fingerpicking of English songwriters like Nick Drake or Richard Thompson, and Ellis's performances are similarly subtle and nuanced, tapping into the bittersweet longing of Chet Baker and the playful poignancy of Bill Evans and Jim Hall. While that might seem surprising coming off 2019's raucous Texas Piano Man, subverting expectations is nothing new for Ellis. Born and raised outside Houston, he gained early acclaim for his piercing introspection and absorbing narratives, but over the course of five solo albums, he flirted with everything from Paul Simon and John Prine to Elton John and Joni Mitchell in a series of sonic and visual transformations that ran the gamut from Redneck Steely Dan to Lone Star Liberace. NPR hailed his , "rdquo" -> musical daring and impeccable songcraft," while Rolling Stone praised his , "rdquo" -> sharp eye for storytelling," and the New York Times lauded his writing as an emotional , "rdquo" -> gut punch." Yesterday's News marks Ellis's debut LP for Niles City Records, an outgrowth of the famed Niles City Sound studio he and longtime collaborator Josh Block run in Fort Worth, TX. title: Collage Poetry Exhibition Donation Drive
description: Do you have old magazines, vintage zines, or leftover craft supplies? We are gathering materials for a community Collage Poetry project that will be turned into a public exhibition. What is Collage Poetry? Collage Poetry weaves together existing text and visual fragments such as magazine cutouts, newspaper snippets, book jackets, zines, school reports/papers, and even non-paper materials (yarn, ribbon, glitter) to form a new, layered work of art. Check out examples from the Alice Notley Artworks collection, like Alone - I Pour a Cup or Vacuum. What to Donate: We are seeking materials in any language, including: Magazines and newspapersBook jackets and zinesOld school reports or papersMixed media (yarn, ribbon, fabric scraps, etc.)Where to Donate: Donations can be dropped off at the collection boxes located in the Service Hubs at Geisel Library and WongAvery Library during each building’s open hours. View Geisel’s hoursView WongAvery’s hours (note: WongAvery is closed on Saturdays)Note: All donations are final and will not be returned. Please ensure all donated papers, reports, or documents are free of sensitive or personal information. We kindly ask that all donations be clean and free of mold, odors, or pests. For safety reasons, please do not donate hazardous materials, including broken glass, chemicals, or sharp metal objects. Questions? Contact us at ucsdlibrary@ucsd.edu.

title: Shaping a Library | Exhibition
description: In early 1970, a San Diego newspaper announced, “Unique Library Taking Shape.” The headline referred to UC San Diego’s Central University Library, now Geisel Library, which was then under construction. The Library’s story began several years earlier. In 1965, architect William L. Pereira was invited to design the Central University Library, envisioned as the flagship building for the UC San Diego campus. Construction began in 1968, and by September 1971, the new Central University Library was dedicated. Over the decades, the building has continued to evolve through expansions and renovations, adapting to the changing needs of the campus community. Tracing the history of the Library’s site design process, construction and expansion from 1965 to 1993, Shaping a Library draws on unique materials from UC San Diego Library’s Special Collections & Archives. From Pereira’s original spherical concept for Geisel Library to Gunnar Birkerts’ glass-walled expansion, architectural drawings, photographs and documents reveal the ideas, people and processes that shaped this beloved campus landmark. Shaping a Library is on view in the Exhibition Gallery on the 2nd (main) Floor of Geisel Library during the building's open hours from Saturday, September 26 through Tuesday, December 8, 2026. Can’t make it to campus to view the exhibition in-person? View the digital exhibit. Image Credit: Architectural rendering of UC San Diego Central University Library, William L. Pereira and Associates, 1965. UC San Diego Library, Special Collections & Archives.

title: The Human Condition: An Exploration of Art & Literature | Exhibit
description: The Human Condition: An Exploration of Art & Literature is an annual art and literary magazine created by medical students for the UC San Diego School of Medicine community. Now in its 32nd year, the student-led publication features art, photography, poetry, prose, sculpture, comics and more, providing a space for safe expression, creativity and exploring identities beyond medicine. This exhibition presents selected works from the 2025 and 2026 issues, offering a glimpse into the experiences, perspectives and creative lives of the School of Medicine community. Visitors are invited to pause, reflect and explore the many dimensions of the human experience. The Human Condition: An Exploration of Art & Literature is on view in the Sally T. WongAvery Library breezeway from September 26 to December 13, 2026, during the building's open hours. Previous issues of The Human Condition magazine, dating back to 2007-08, are available to download and read at your leisure. Curated by: Amy Xue, MS4, editor-in-chief, 2026-27 Myat Wai, MS4, editor-in-chief, 2026-27Supported by: UC San Diego School of MedicineUC San Diego Library

Image taken from "A Map to the Next World" by 2019-2022 Poet Laureate Joy Harjo. Harjo was the first Native American Poet Laureate and centered her term on celebrating indigenous poetry and voices with her project "Living Nations, Living Worlds."

title: Library Milestones | Exhibit
description: Before the rise of digital publications and licensed electronic resources, academic libraries measured the size of their collections by the number of physical volumes on their shelves. Reaching a million-volume milestone was a source of pride and a mark of growth. This exhibit highlights five titles that mark milestones in the growth of the UC San Diego Library’s physical collections. Together, they also reflect the generosity of donors and support groups who helped build the collections and offer a glimpse into what made a book milestone-worthy at the time. Library Milestones is on view outside of Special Collections & Archives on the 2nd (main) Floor of Geisel Library during the building's open hours through Sunday, December 13, 2026. Photo citation: John Ogilby. America: being the latest, and most accurate description of the New World; containing the original inhabitants, and the remarkable voyages thither... London: printed by the author, 1671. UC San Diego Library, Special Collections & Archives.

Día de los Muertos, or Day of the Dead, is a Mexican tradition that honors and remembers loved ones who have passed. At the heart of the celebration are remembrance, family, and community. As part of the museum’s celebration, guests will have the opportunity to experience traditional elements of Día de los Muertos while surrounded by some of the world’s most beautiful and historic vehicles.

description: The Art Glass Guild will be hosting their 2026 Fall Patio Show and Sale on October 10th and 11th. Visitors will see the patio full of juried artists exhibiting their creations as they stroll through Spanish Village Art Center in Balboa Park. Beautiful art glass exhibiting techniques such as: blown, fused, torch, stained, cast, and etched will be on display with the artist right there to explain or show how it is done. There will be entertainment for all including, a demonstration featuring torch-work, as well as an area for children and adults alike to create their own unique mosaic art piece to take home. The Art Glass Guild is a non-profit art education center, focused on supporting local glass artists as well as other San Diego non-profits with art related programs benefiting the community. “This is a fun family outing to see an array of beautiful art glass, glass demonstrations and free mosaic make and take and also to support our local artists,” says Helen Munroe, Fused Glass Artist and member of The Art Glass Guild. address: 2001 Pan American Plaza, San Diego, CA, 92101
description: Get ready for a day of engineering, coding, creativity, and flying pumpkins! Pumpkin Chunkin’ is returning to the San Diego Air & Space Museum on October 10, from 10 am to 1 pm bringing hands-on STEM challenges and plenty of Halloween fun for kids and families. This year, we’re excited to welcome a local high school robotics team, who will show visitors some of their amazing robot creations and demonstrate what goes into designing, building, and coding a competition robot. Young engineers can then try their own hand at solving Halloween-themed challenges throughout the museum. Activities will include: Build a Catapult: Design and construct a catapult, then see how far you can launch a candy pumpkin! Pumpkin Parachutes: Create a parachute designed to help a pumpkin make a safe landing. 3D Pen Spider Webs: Experiment with 3D pens to create creepy-crawly spider webs. Code a Mouse: Program a robotic mouse to navigate its way through a maze. Create a Monster: Use if-then statements to design a monster that reacts to different situations. And, of course, the highlight of Pumpkin Chunkin’ is the moment everyone waits for the PUMPKIN DROP! Watch as pumpkins take flight in a spectacular finale that combines a little Halloween fun with a lot of physics and engineering. There will be one small difference this year: the museum is currently covered in scaffolding as part of ongoing work on the building. So a new and exciting pumpkin platform will be used. Halloween Fun for Everyone Pumpkin Chunkin’ is included with museum admission, and October is Kids Free Month at the San Diego Air & Space Museum! During October, up to two children per one paid adult admission can visit the museum for free. Youth groups are welcome, too! Groups of 10–25 youth and their chaperones can attend for free with advance registration. To preregister your group, email education@sdasm.org . Costumes are welcome! Come dressed as your favorite astronaut, scientist, robot, monster, or anything else you can imagine. Join us for Pumpkin Chunkin’ and discover that some of the best Halloween fun comes with a little engineering mixed in!

Whether you are fishing or not, participate in the art of gyotaku and print your own fish with simple ink and paper. Backed by his band The Stranger, Levittown, NY native Mike Santoro?s fingers flash up and down the keys before he jumps up to grab the mic to belt out such high-energy Billy Joel classics as ?Uptown Girl? and ?Only the Good Die Young.? For the second half of the roughly three-hour show, Ronnie Smith dons the iconic sunglasses and bedazzled suits of Elton John as he charts his style from the ?70s to the present. Bittersweet anthems such as ?Rocket Man (I Think It?s Going to Be a Long, Long Time)? mix with more whimsical material such as ?Crocodile Rock? and the fictional rock-group narrative ?Bennie and the Jets.? During each engaging, interactive show, both acts aim to channel the spirit of their originals so well that audiences will forget they?re a tribute!

description: Longevity in music comes through pushing yourself and expanding the possibilities of your sound. This has never been more true for Copeland. The band, which originally formed in Lakeland, Florida in 2001, has unveiled six albums, spanning from their 2003s debut Beneath Medicine Tree to 2016s Ixora. While they began as a rock band, Copelands music has explored multiple genres and pulled in various stylistic influences like electronic and symphonic. In the past the musicians have aptly melded these styles, creating a unique amalgam of sounds. This time they wanted to take each sound and style and push it to its logical extreme.

title: Armand Hammer with Quelle Chris and Open Mike Eagle
description: For nearly a decade as a duo, and longer still as solo artists, Armand Hammer have left a palpable mark on modern rap and hip-hop. At turns both sharp-witted and soul-crushing, their lyrics unspool threads of socio-political, historical, and philosophical import with a potent blend of incisive critique, gallows humor, and narrative élan. Mercy is the first Armand Hammer album since 2023's We Buy Diabetic Test Strips, a project that The Observer (UK) described as "an exceptional record that deserves your time and headphones" and The Line Of Best Fit deemed "their headiest and most impressive work thus far." On 2021's Haram, their first with The Alchemist, the duo "drag postcolonial wounds onto the examination table" (Pitchfork). Beats Per Minute called it "a tremendous success." Earlier this year, billy woods released GOLLIWOG, ", "rdquo" -> a densely poetic, totally masterful tour de force" (Rolling Stone) and "one of 2025's truly essential albums" (The FADER). Meanwhile, ELUCID's "enthralling" (MOJO) 2024 album REVELATOR was described by Pitchfork as "soul food for those who know a better world is possible if we're willing to fight for it." The New York Times, in naming REVELATOR one of their Best Albums Of 2024, called it "a dense, overdriven, fiercely abrasive album that cranks up the tradition of Public Enemy's Bomb Squad productions for 21st-century impact."

title: Collage Poetry Exhibition Donation Drive
description: Do you have old magazines, vintage zines, or leftover craft supplies? We are gathering materials for a community Collage Poetry project that will be turned into a public exhibition. What is Collage Poetry? Collage Poetry weaves together existing text and visual fragments such as magazine cutouts, newspaper snippets, book jackets, zines, school reports/papers, and even non-paper materials (yarn, ribbon, glitter) to form a new, layered work of art. Check out examples from the Alice Notley Artworks collection, like Alone - I Pour a Cup or Vacuum. What to Donate: We are seeking materials in any language, including: Magazines and newspapersBook jackets and zinesOld school reports or papersMixed media (yarn, ribbon, fabric scraps, etc.)Where to Donate: Donations can be dropped off at the collection boxes located in the Service Hubs at Geisel Library and WongAvery Library during each building’s open hours. View Geisel’s hoursView WongAvery’s hours (note: WongAvery is closed on Saturdays)Note: All donations are final and will not be returned. Please ensure all donated papers, reports, or documents are free of sensitive or personal information. We kindly ask that all donations be clean and free of mold, odors, or pests. For safety reasons, please do not donate hazardous materials, including broken glass, chemicals, or sharp metal objects. Questions? Contact us at ucsdlibrary@ucsd.edu.

title: Shaping a Library | Exhibition
description: In early 1970, a San Diego newspaper announced, “Unique Library Taking Shape.” The headline referred to UC San Diego’s Central University Library, now Geisel Library, which was then under construction. The Library’s story began several years earlier. In 1965, architect William L. Pereira was invited to design the Central University Library, envisioned as the flagship building for the UC San Diego campus. Construction began in 1968, and by September 1971, the new Central University Library was dedicated. Over the decades, the building has continued to evolve through expansions and renovations, adapting to the changing needs of the campus community. Tracing the history of the Library’s site design process, construction and expansion from 1965 to 1993, Shaping a Library draws on unique materials from UC San Diego Library’s Special Collections & Archives. From Pereira’s original spherical concept for Geisel Library to Gunnar Birkerts’ glass-walled expansion, architectural drawings, photographs and documents reveal the ideas, people and processes that shaped this beloved campus landmark. Shaping a Library is on view in the Exhibition Gallery on the 2nd (main) Floor of Geisel Library during the building's open hours from Saturday, September 26 through Tuesday, December 8, 2026. Can’t make it to campus to view the exhibition in-person? View the digital exhibit. Image Credit: Architectural rendering of UC San Diego Central University Library, William L. Pereira and Associates, 1965. UC San Diego Library, Special Collections & Archives.

title: The Human Condition: An Exploration of Art & Literature | Exhibit
description: The Human Condition: An Exploration of Art & Literature is an annual art and literary magazine created by medical students for the UC San Diego School of Medicine community. Now in its 32nd year, the student-led publication features art, photography, poetry, prose, sculpture, comics and more, providing a space for safe expression, creativity and exploring identities beyond medicine. This exhibition presents selected works from the 2025 and 2026 issues, offering a glimpse into the experiences, perspectives and creative lives of the School of Medicine community. Visitors are invited to pause, reflect and explore the many dimensions of the human experience. The Human Condition: An Exploration of Art & Literature is on view in the Sally T. WongAvery Library breezeway from September 26 to December 13, 2026, during the building's open hours. Previous issues of The Human Condition magazine, dating back to 2007-08, are available to download and read at your leisure. Curated by: Amy Xue, MS4, editor-in-chief, 2026-27 Myat Wai, MS4, editor-in-chief, 2026-27Supported by: UC San Diego School of MedicineUC San Diego Library

title: Library Milestones | Exhibit
description: Before the rise of digital publications and licensed electronic resources, academic libraries measured the size of their collections by the number of physical volumes on their shelves. Reaching a million-volume milestone was a source of pride and a mark of growth. This exhibit highlights five titles that mark milestones in the growth of the UC San Diego Library’s physical collections. Together, they also reflect the generosity of donors and support groups who helped build the collections and offer a glimpse into what made a book milestone-worthy at the time. Library Milestones is on view outside of Special Collections & Archives on the 2nd (main) Floor of Geisel Library during the building's open hours through Sunday, December 13, 2026. Photo citation: John Ogilby. America: being the latest, and most accurate description of the New World; containing the original inhabitants, and the remarkable voyages thither... London: printed by the author, 1671. UC San Diego Library, Special Collections & Archives.

Beautiful art glass exhibiting techniques such as: blown, fused, torch, stained, cast, and etched will be on display with the artist right there to explain or show how it is done. There will be entertainment for all including, a demonstration featuring torch-work, as well as an area for children and adults alike to create their own unique mosaic art piece to take home. The Art Glass Guild is a non-profit art education center, focused on supporting local glass artists as well as other San Diego non-profits with art related programs benefiting the community. “This is a fun family outing to see an array of beautiful art glass, glass demonstrations and free mosaic make and take and also to support our local artists,” says Helen Munroe, Fused Glass Artist and member of The Art Glass Guild. title: Interpol - North America Tour 2026 with DIIV
description: This Mirror Weighs a Ton, finds the band turning inward while continuing to move forward. Across the record, reflection, distortion and perception become a lens through which familiar shapes are refracted into something slightly alien, as if seen through a different kind of light. Synthesizers, strings, acoustic guitars and percussion are integrated into the fabric of the songs, expanding the palette while revealing colors already latent within it. Nothing feels imposed. Instead, the additions deepen the band?s language of restraint, atmosphere and tension. The result is an album that feels expansive, uncanny and alive with forward motion, not a reinvention but an evolution that allows Interpol to continue transforming without losing their identity.

description: One of the lynchpins of Chicagos flourishing songwriter scene is Steve Dawson, a songwriter and vocalist who elevates everything he touches. - WBEZ Chicago An evocative, brilliant songwriter who imbues his songs and recordings with folk, country, and a smattering of soul he should, by all rights, be a household name. - Popmatters Steve Dawson will look back over 35 years of songs and music making, including songs from his first Chicago band, Stump The Host, through Dolly Varden, Funeral Bonsai Wedding and up to his more recent critically acclaimed solo albums, Ghosts, and At The Bottom of a Canyon in the Branches of a Tree. Over the course of 6 albums with Dolly Varden, 4 solo albums, and 2 albums with the jazz / folk combo, Funeral Bonsai Wedding, Dawson has delved into all corners of American music and dug deep into the mysteries and wonders of life, mortality, love and memory. Dawson will be joined by a few guest musicians for this evenings show. Originally from San Diego, California, he spent his teen years in Hailey, Idaho, where he learned guitar and started writing songs. After a few years at the Berklee School of Music in Boston, Dawson moved to Chicago and formed the band, Stump the Host, with his future wife, artist and singer, Diane Christiansen. Later he formed, recorded and toured with Dolly Varden and Funeral Bonsai Wedding. More recently he has created critically acclaimed solo albums for the Pravda record label. Dawson also teaches songwriting at the legendary Old Town School of Folk Music and co-wrote a book on songwriting and the creative process with Mark Caro called, Take It To The Bridge: Unlocking The Great Songs Inside You. In 2020 Dawson was awarded the Esteemed Artist Award from the City of Chicago.

title: BEAT: Belew/Vai/Levin/Bozzio Performing the Music of KING CRIMSON
description: Following more than 100 acclaimed performances across North and South America, Europe, and Japan, BEAT returns this fall for the last North American tour. Former King Crimson members Adrian Belew and Tony Levin are joined by guitar virtuoso Steve Vai and legendary drummer Terry Bozzio to perform the music of the three landmark 1980s King Crimson albums---Discipline, Beat, and Three of a Perfect Pair. Rather than attempting to recreate the original recordings, BEAT brings this extraordinary music to life with the spirit, precision, and adventurousness that made it so enduring. Whether you've lived with these albums for decades or are discovering them for the first time, this is the final opportunity to experience one of progressive music's most celebrated catalogs performed by four of the best musicians on the planet.

title: Collage Poetry Exhibition Donation Drive
description: Do you have old magazines, vintage zines, or leftover craft supplies? We are gathering materials for a community Collage Poetry project that will be turned into a public exhibition. What is Collage Poetry? Collage Poetry weaves together existing text and visual fragments such as magazine cutouts, newspaper snippets, book jackets, zines, school reports/papers, and even non-paper materials (yarn, ribbon, glitter) to form a new, layered work of art. Check out examples from the Alice Notley Artworks collection, like Alone - I Pour a Cup or Vacuum. What to Donate: We are seeking materials in any language, including: Magazines and newspapersBook jackets and zinesOld school reports or papersMixed media (yarn, ribbon, fabric scraps, etc.)Where to Donate: Donations can be dropped off at the collection boxes located in the Service Hubs at Geisel Library and WongAvery Library during each building’s open hours. View Geisel’s hoursView WongAvery’s hours (note: WongAvery is closed on Saturdays)Note: All donations are final and will not be returned. Please ensure all donated papers, reports, or documents are free of sensitive or personal information. We kindly ask that all donations be clean and free of mold, odors, or pests. For safety reasons, please do not donate hazardous materials, including broken glass, chemicals, or sharp metal objects. Questions? Contact us at ucsdlibrary@ucsd.edu.

title: Shaping a Library | Exhibition
description: In early 1970, a San Diego newspaper announced, “Unique Library Taking Shape.” The headline referred to UC San Diego’s Central University Library, now Geisel Library, which was then under construction. The Library’s story began several years earlier. In 1965, architect William L. Pereira was invited to design the Central University Library, envisioned as the flagship building for the UC San Diego campus. Construction began in 1968, and by September 1971, the new Central University Library was dedicated. Over the decades, the building has continued to evolve through expansions and renovations, adapting to the changing needs of the campus community. Tracing the history of the Library’s site design process, construction and expansion from 1965 to 1993, Shaping a Library draws on unique materials from UC San Diego Library’s Special Collections & Archives. From Pereira’s original spherical concept for Geisel Library to Gunnar Birkerts’ glass-walled expansion, architectural drawings, photographs and documents reveal the ideas, people and processes that shaped this beloved campus landmark. Shaping a Library is on view in the Exhibition Gallery on the 2nd (main) Floor of Geisel Library during the building's open hours from Saturday, September 26 through Tuesday, December 8, 2026. Can’t make it to campus to view the exhibition in-person? View the digital exhibit. Image Credit: Architectural rendering of UC San Diego Central University Library, William L. Pereira and Associates, 1965. UC San Diego Library, Special Collections & Archives.

title: The Human Condition: An Exploration of Art & Literature | Exhibit
description: The Human Condition: An Exploration of Art & Literature is an annual art and literary magazine created by medical students for the UC San Diego School of Medicine community. Now in its 32nd year, the student-led publication features art, photography, poetry, prose, sculpture, comics and more, providing a space for safe expression, creativity and exploring identities beyond medicine. This exhibition presents selected works from the 2025 and 2026 issues, offering a glimpse into the experiences, perspectives and creative lives of the School of Medicine community. Visitors are invited to pause, reflect and explore the many dimensions of the human experience. The Human Condition: An Exploration of Art & Literature is on view in the Sally T. WongAvery Library breezeway from September 26 to December 13, 2026, during the building's open hours. Previous issues of The Human Condition magazine, dating back to 2007-08, are available to download and read at your leisure. Curated by: Amy Xue, MS4, editor-in-chief, 2026-27 Myat Wai, MS4, editor-in-chief, 2026-27Supported by: UC San Diego School of MedicineUC San Diego Library

title: Library Milestones | Exhibit
description: Before the rise of digital publications and licensed electronic resources, academic libraries measured the size of their collections by the number of physical volumes on their shelves. Reaching a million-volume milestone was a source of pride and a mark of growth. This exhibit highlights five titles that mark milestones in the growth of the UC San Diego Library’s physical collections. Together, they also reflect the generosity of donors and support groups who helped build the collections and offer a glimpse into what made a book milestone-worthy at the time. Library Milestones is on view outside of Special Collections & Archives on the 2nd (main) Floor of Geisel Library during the building's open hours through Sunday, December 13, 2026. Photo citation: John Ogilby. America: being the latest, and most accurate description of the New World; containing the original inhabitants, and the remarkable voyages thither... title: Shaping a Library | Exhibition
description: In early 1970, a San Diego newspaper announced, “Unique Library Taking Shape.” The headline referred to UC San Diego’s Central University Library, now Geisel Library, which was then under construction. The Library’s story began several years earlier. In 1965, architect William L. Pereira was invited to design the Central University Library, envisioned as the flagship building for the UC San Diego campus. Construction began in 1968, and by September 1971, the new Central University Library was dedicated. Over the decades, the building has continued to evolve through expansions and renovations, adapting to the changing needs of the campus community. Tracing the history of the Library’s site design process, construction and expansion from 1965 to 1993, Shaping a Library draws on unique materials from UC San Diego Library’s Special Collections & Archives. From Pereira’s original spherical concept for Geisel Library to Gunnar Birkerts’ glass-walled expansion, architectural drawings, photographs and documents reveal the ideas, people and processes that shaped this beloved campus landmark. Shaping a Library is on view in the Exhibition Gallery on the 2nd (main) Floor of Geisel Library during the building's open hours from Saturday, September 26 through Tuesday, December 8, 2026. Can’t make it to campus to view the exhibition in-person? View the digital exhibit. Image Credit: Architectural rendering of UC San Diego Central University Library, William L. Pereira and Associates, 1965. UC San Diego Library, Special Collections & Archives.

This exhibition presents selected works from the 2025 and 2026 issues, offering a glimpse into the experiences, perspectives and creative lives of the School of Medicine community. Visitors are invited to pause, reflect and explore the many dimensions of the human experience. The Human Condition: An Exploration of Art & Literature is on view in the Sally T. WongAvery Library breezeway from September 26 to December 13, 2026, during the building's open hours. Previous issues of The Human Condition magazine, dating back to 2007-08, are available to download and read at your leisure. Curated by: Amy Xue, MS4, editor-in-chief, 2026-27 Myat Wai, MS4, editor-in-chief, 2026-27Supported by: UC San Diego School of MedicineUC San Diego Library

title: Library Milestones | Exhibit
description: Before the rise of digital publications and licensed electronic resources, academic libraries measured the size of their collections by the number of physical volumes on their shelves. Together, they also reflect the generosity of donors and support groups who helped build the collections and offer a glimpse into what made a book milestone-worthy at the time. Library Milestones is on view outside of Special Collections & Archives on the 2nd (main) Floor of Geisel Library during the building's open hours through Sunday, December 13, 2026. Photo citation: John Ogilby. America: being the latest, and most accurate description of the New World; containing the original inhabitants, and the remarkable voyages thither... London: printed by the author, 1671. UC San Diego Library, Special Collections & Archives.

title: White Denim w. Arc Iris
description: Ive always wanted to make work thats a reflection of my life experience, says singer-guitarist James Petralli, leader of venturous L.A.-based rockers White Denim. The just-below-the-surface significance to 13 as an album title is that I was born on the thirteenth of August. 13 in numerology can signify independence, creativity, and a solid foundation, but inversely is often considered to be unlucky and can signify chaos and misfortune. Like everyone, I can certainly see both sides in my life.13 also happens to be the thirteenth album of White Denims career. An incandescent, groove-heavy alchemy of rock, funk, dub, soul and down-dirty blues and plenty more besides its imbued with the same questing spirit thats been the bands trademark since first starting in Austin, Texas, some 20 years ago.Petrallis wide-ranging musical appetites have become more voracious over time. The sounds and textures of 13 are informed by everyone from Scritti Politti to The Gap Band, Terry Reid to King Tubby, Caetano Veloso to John Cale, Stevie Wonder to 80s-era Steve Winwood. Such diversity is reflected in multi-faceted gems like (God Created) Lock And Key, Only A Fool and Thats Rap.The seed of the project is rooted in the irresistible Chew Nails. Its a straightforward glam-rock tune, says Petralli. My take on the New York Groove, which is itself a take on the Bo Diddley beat. It has a big ol guitar riff and a singalong chorus. Its familiar territory for me, yet the vocal is perhaps more forward than most things Ive done for the band. Its the song that made me feel like I was definitely making a White Denim album.The duality of 13 is immediately apparent. The pungent funk-blues of opener (God Created) Lock And Key begins with a piece of waggish self-mythology On the thirteenth day God created White Denim but soon goes somewhere darker. This is a Beefheart / Sun Ra sort of thing, Petralli explains. I hope that its a somewhat terrifying, startling, and visceral piece for everyone that hears it. Everything I say in that song is the truth. Its about power, generational cycles of abuse, shame, violence, and survival. The things that we all understand and know and see and push down to get through the day.

It is the musical you know and love, but dragged through a cloud of strawberry scented vapor and a TikTok filter. It's the show that you want (Ooh! Ooh! Ooh, honey!) Don't miss the Chicago premiere of this hit musical, straight from NYC. GREASE is no longer the word. Now the word is VAPE! - New York Post A must-see! A fun, irreverent night out. title: Collage Poetry Exhibition Donation Drive
description: Do you have old magazines, vintage zines, or leftover craft supplies? We are gathering materials for a community Collage Poetry project that will be turned into a public exhibition. What is Collage Poetry? Collage Poetry weaves together existing text and visual fragments such as magazine cutouts, newspaper snippets, book jackets, zines, school reports/papers, and even non-paper materials (yarn, ribbon, glitter) to form a new, layered work of art. Check out examples from the Alice Notley Artworks collection, like Alone - I Pour a Cup or Vacuum. What to Donate: We are seeking materials in any language, including: Magazines and newspapersBook jackets and zinesOld school reports or papersMixed media (yarn, ribbon, fabric scraps, etc.)Where to Donate: Donations can be dropped off at the collection boxes located in the Service Hubs at Geisel Library and WongAvery Library during each building’s open hours. View Geisel’s hoursView WongAvery’s hours (note: WongAvery is closed on Saturdays)Note: All donations are final and will not be returned. Please ensure all donated papers, reports, or documents are free of sensitive or personal information. We kindly ask that all donations be clean and free of mold, odors, or pests. For safety reasons, please do not donate hazardous materials, including broken glass, chemicals, or sharp metal objects. Questions? Contact us at ucsdlibrary@ucsd.edu.

title: Shaping a Library | Exhibition
description: In early 1970, a San Diego newspaper announced, “Unique Library Taking Shape.” The headline referred to UC San Diego’s Central University Library, now Geisel Library, which was then under construction. The Library’s story began several years earlier. In 1965, architect William L. Pereira was invited to design the Central University Library, envisioned as the flagship building for the UC San Diego campus. Construction began in 1968, and by September 1971, the new Central University Library was dedicated. Over the decades, the building has continued to evolve through expansions and renovations, adapting to the changing needs of the campus community. Tracing the history of the Library’s site design process, construction and expansion from 1965 to 1993, Shaping a Library draws on unique materials from UC San Diego Library’s Special Collections & Archives. From Pereira’s original spherical concept for Geisel Library to Gunnar Birkerts’ glass-walled expansion, architectural drawings, photographs and documents reveal the ideas, people and processes that shaped this beloved campus landmark. Shaping a Library is on view in the Exhibition Gallery on the 2nd (main) Floor of Geisel Library during the building's open hours from Saturday, September 26 through Tuesday, December 8, 2026. Can’t make it to campus to view the exhibition in-person? View the digital exhibit. Image Credit: Architectural rendering of UC San Diego Central University Library, William L. Pereira and Associates, 1965. UC San Diego Library, Special Collections & Archives.

title: The Human Condition: An Exploration of Art & Literature | Exhibit
description: The Human Condition: An Exploration of Art & Literature is an annual art and literary magazine created by medical students for the UC San Diego School of Medicine community. Now in its 32nd year, the student-led publication features art, photography, poetry, prose, sculpture, comics and more, providing a space for safe expression, creativity and exploring identities beyond medicine. This exhibition presents selected works from the 2025 and 2026 issues, offering a glimpse into the experiences, perspectives and creative lives of the School of Medicine community. Visitors are invited to pause, reflect and explore the many dimensions of the human experience. The Human Condition: An Exploration of Art & Literature is on view in the Sally T. WongAvery Library breezeway from September 26 to December 13, 2026, during the building's open hours. Previous issues of The Human Condition magazine, dating back to 2007-08, are available to download and read at your leisure. Curated by: Amy Xue, MS4, editor-in-chief, 2026-27 Myat Wai, MS4, editor-in-chief, 2026-27Supported by: UC San Diego School of MedicineUC San Diego Library

title: Library Milestones | Exhibit
description: Before the rise of digital publications and licensed electronic resources, academic libraries measured the size of their collections by the number of physical volumes on their shelves. Reaching a million-volume milestone was a source of pride and a mark of growth. This exhibit highlights five titles that mark milestones in the growth of the UC San Diego Library’s physical collections. Together, they also reflect the generosity of donors and support groups who helped build the collections and offer a glimpse into what made a book milestone-worthy at the time. Library Milestones is on view outside of Special Collections & Archives on the 2nd (main) Floor of Geisel Library during the building's open hours through Sunday, December 13, 2026. Photo citation: John Ogilby. America: being the latest, and most accurate description of the New World; containing the original inhabitants, and the remarkable voyages thither... London: printed by the author, 1671. UC San Diego Library, Special Collections & Archives.

description: Vape! The Grease Parody is a hilariously unhinged spoof of the iconic and timeless musical film Grease. The hair products may have changed, but the drama, the rivalries, and the thirst for hallway clout remain timeless. It is the musical you know and love, but dragged through a cloud of strawberry scented vapor and a TikTok filter. It's the show that you want (Ooh! Ooh! Ooh, honey!) I couldn't stop laughing. - Hollywood Press Corps VAPE! is the one that you want! Clever, goofy and camp. - Theater Pizzazz Brash, fast and unapologetically smart. - Theaterscene.net VAPE! The Grease Parody is 85 minutes with no intermission.

title: Neon Chicha: Counter‑Aesthetics from Peruvian Pop(ular) Art
description: Presentation by Alfredo Villar on Peruvian Contemporary Pop Art and Its Relation to Migrant Movements, with an Emphasis on Chicha Art and joined in moderated conversation with the artist, MONKY. Followed by a DJ set of Peruvian Chicha. In his discussion, Alfredo will explore how chicha graphics emerged as the first great visual conquest of a mass that overflowed, invading cities and transforming their peripheries into new centers of creativity. He will address the movement's roots in internal migration, its popular aesthetic, and its significance as a form of cultural resistance and identity formation. Presented in partnership with ArtPower, House of Peru, Sixth College, Muir College, Theater & Dance Dept, VisArts Dept

title: Shaping a Library | Exhibition
description: In early 1970, a San Diego newspaper announced, “Unique Library Taking Shape.” The headline referred to UC San Diego’s Central University Library, now Geisel Library, which was then under construction. The Library’s story began several years earlier. In 1965, architect William L. Pereira was invited to design the Central University Library, envisioned as the flagship building for the UC San Diego campus. Construction began in 1968, and by September 1971, the new Central University Library was dedicated. Over the decades, the building has continued to evolve through expansions and renovations, adapting to the changing needs of the campus community. Tracing the history of the Library’s site design process, construction and expansion from 1965 to 1993, Shaping a Library draws on unique materials from UC San Diego Library’s Special Collections & Archives. From Pereira’s original spherical concept for Geisel Library to Gunnar Birkerts’ glass-walled expansion, architectural drawings, photographs and documents reveal the ideas, people and processes that shaped this beloved campus landmark. Shaping a Library is on view in the Exhibition Gallery on the 2nd (main) Floor of Geisel Library during the building's open hours from Saturday, September 26 through Tuesday, December 8, 2026. Can’t make it to campus to view the exhibition in-person? View the digital exhibit. Image Credit: Architectural rendering of UC San Diego Central University Library, William L. Pereira and Associates, 1965. UC San Diego Library, Special Collections & Archives.

title: Arts and Humanities Futures Studies: An Exploratory Symposium
description: The Arts and Humanities Futures Studies Exploratory Symposium will bring together faculty and invited experts to consider how artistic and humanistic inquiry can help society navigate long-term technological, political, environmental and cultural change. Drawing on history, philosophy, literature, the visual and performing arts, and ethics, the symposium will explore how understanding the past and critically examining the present can expand our capacity beyond just what is probable, but to imagine possible, preferable, and more humane futures. The symposium will introduce participants to the interdisciplinary field of Futures Studies and approaches including foresight and backcasting, scenario development, systems thinking, and speculative inquiry. Rather than attempting to predict a single future, Futures Studies considers multiple trajectories and asks fundamental questions about the choices, values, institutions and ideas that shape them. Through presentations, interdisciplinary conversations, and collaborative working sessions, participants will examine the future of democracy and civic life; artificial intelligence and the human consequences of emerging technologies; ethics, rights, and human agency; climate and environmental change; culture, creativity, and storytelling; and the changing nature of work, education, relationships, and meaningful lives. Together, these subjects invite a larger question: How can the arts and humanities help society envision — and work toward — futures in which people and communities can flourish? The symposium is exploratory by design. It will showcase existing faculty inquiry and creative practice, develop new connections across disciplines, and invite participants to help define the intellectual priorities and appropriate structure of a broader Arts and Humanities Futures Studies Initiative at UC San Diego. Possibilities emerging from this exploration may include interdisciplinary research collaborations, creative projects, public and community programming, international partnerships, student-learning opportunities, and new avenues for external research support. At its center is a fundamental proposition: the future is not solely a technological question. It is also a historical, ethical, cultural and imaginative one — and the arts and humanities are essential not only to understanding what may lie ahead, but to asking what kinds of futures we should seek to create. title: Library Milestones | Exhibit
description: Before the rise of digital publications and licensed electronic resources, academic libraries measured the size of their collections by the number of physical volumes on their shelves. Together, they also reflect the generosity of donors and support groups who helped build the collections and offer a glimpse into what made a book milestone-worthy at the time. title: Coffee and Conversations
description: Join co-editors Océane Boulais and Theodora Mautz for a conversation about the community-led zine in situ, born at Scripps Institution of Oceanography. Discover how graduate students, postdocs, and staff transform scientific experiences—from coral reef surveys and whale encounters to ice cores and lab life—into visual art, photography, poetry, and multimedia storytelling for the zine. Proceeds from the zine and community support go toward printing costs, art supplies, and events that keep collective creative action alive at Scripps, making in situ as much a grassroots organizing effort as a publication. Océane and Theodora will share the evolution of in situ , from its inaugural Seas of Change issue to its current Countercurrents volume, and explore how creative expression can complement scientific inquiry, build community across disciplines, and offer new ways of understanding our oceans. Stay for the end of the presentation, where a surprise instrument invites you to play the ocean’s frequencies yourself! The talk will take place at Mingei International Museum. Theodora Mautz is a PhD candidate in the Marine Biology program at Scripps Institution of Oceanography. She currently researches cephalopod reproduction. Océane Boulais is a PhD candidate in the Applied Ocean Science program at Scripps Institution of Oceanography. As an ecoacoustician, Océane listens to the ocean as a language of texture, color, and rhythm and then employs instruments to broadcast sound from healthy coral reefs into restoration reef sites, drawing coral and fish larvae home by sound via “acoustic enrichment”.
