title: PARA/normal Borders Conversation II: Sky Hopinka + Maggie Nelson
venue: Qualcomm Institute's CALIT2 Auditorium in Atkinson Hall
description: Sky Hopinka + Maggie Nelson Part II of the PARA/normal Borders Conversation Series Through film, writing, and critical inquiry, Sky Hopinka and Maggie Nelson explore how artistic practice becomes a way of knowing. Working across experimental film, creative nonfiction, philosophy, and visual culture, their presentations of individual work and conversation will consider how memory, perception, language, and embodied experience shape our understanding of place, history, and one another. Together, they will examine how art creates new ways of seeing, remembering, and imagining the world. PARA/normal Borders is the 2026–27 edition of the MexiCali Biennial, a multidisciplinary exhibition and public humanities initiative exploring the borderlands as a space where visible and invisible histories converge. Rather than treating the border solely as a geopolitical boundary, the project approaches it as a cultural, psychological, ecological, and technological condition that shapes contemporary life. Inspired by the concept of the borderlands as a “thin place,” PARA/normal Borders considers how migration, language, memory, Indigenous knowledge, media, surveillance, and speculative futures intersect across the California–Mexico border region. Through exhibitions, performances, publications, research initiatives, and public conversations, the Biennial invites artists, writers, scholars, and communities to examine the many ways borders continue to influence how we remember, imagine, and inhabit the world. The PARA/normal Borders Conversation Series brings together MacArthur Fellows whose work expands our understanding of borders across literature, film, visual art, music, and critical scholarship. This program is co-presented by the MexiCali Biennial and the University of California, San Diego Department of Literature’s New Writing Series, in partnership with the University of California, San Diego Geisel Library’s Archive for New Poetry, Department of Visual Arts, Indigenous Futures Institute, and Gallery QI. This event is free and open to the public. A public reception will immediately follow the event. Please RSVP by Monday, October 12, 2026. → Learn more about PARA/normal Borders Discussion I: Josh Kun + Alex Rivera → Learn more about PARA/normal Borders Discussion III: Cristina Rivera Garza + Fred Moten

title: Kelly Akashi: Artist Talk
description: The Department of Visual Arts is pleased to welcome Kelly Akashi as this year's Longenecker-Roth Artist-in-Residence! With deft manual skill and deep material knowledge, Kelly Akashi’s visual language emphasizes the impermanence of the natural world, recording and indexing fragmented moments in time. Her practice is characterized by a rigorous conceptual approach, yet the work is distinguished by a deep reverence for process. Always a student, Akashi continually studies new practices and physical techniques, including glass-blowing, flame-working, casting, candle-making, and stone carving. Born in Los Angeles in 1983, she holds a BFA from Otis College of Art & Design, an MFA from the University of Southern California, and studied at the Städelschule in Frankfurt. Recent institutional solo exhibitions include the San Jose Museum of Art, Frye Art Museum, Museum of Contemporary Art San Diego, Henry Art Gallery, SculptureCenter, and Galleria d’Arte Moderna di Milano, among others. Public commissions include a monumental installation for JFK International Airport’s New Terminal One, the Hyundai Terrace for the 2026 Whitney Biennial, an upcoming outdoor sculpture commission for Williams College Museum of Art, and projects with the Aspen Art Museum and the Clark Art Institute. She is the recipient of the 2024 Distinguished Women in the Arts Award from MOCA Los Angeles, as well as grants from the Trellis Art Fund, Andy Warhol Foundation, LACMA Art + Tech, Peter S. Reed Foundation, and Tieger Foundation. Akashi serves as Core Faculty in Grad Art at ArtCenter College of Design, and in 2025 was selected as an Artist in Residence at Pilchuck Glass School.

title: Collage Poetry Exhibition Donation Drive
description: Do you have old magazines, vintage zines, or leftover craft supplies? We are gathering materials for a community Collage Poetry project that will be turned into a public exhibition. What is Collage Poetry? Collage Poetry weaves together existing text and visual fragments such as magazine cutouts, newspaper snippets, book jackets, zines, school reports/papers, and even non-paper materials (yarn, ribbon, glitter) to form a new, layered work of art. Check out examples from the Alice Notley Artworks collection, like Alone - I Pour a Cup or Vacuum. What to Donate: We are seeking materials in any language, including: Magazines and newspapersBook jackets and zinesOld school reports or papersMixed media (yarn, ribbon, fabric scraps, etc.)Where to Donate: Donations can be dropped off at the collection boxes located in the Service Hubs at Geisel Library and WongAvery Library during each building’s open hours. View Geisel’s hoursView WongAvery’s hours (note: WongAvery is closed on Saturdays)Note: All donations are final and will not be returned. Please ensure all donated papers, reports, or documents are free of sensitive or personal information. We kindly ask that all donations be clean and free of mold, odors, or pests. For safety reasons, please do not donate hazardous materials, including broken glass, chemicals, or sharp metal objects. Questions? Contact us at ucsdlibrary@ucsd.edu.

title: Shaping a Library | Exhibition
description: In early 1970, a San Diego newspaper announced, “Unique Library Taking Shape.” The headline referred to UC San Diego’s Central University Library, now Geisel Library, which was then under construction. The Library’s story began several years earlier. In 1965, architect William L. Pereira was invited to design the Central University Library, envisioned as the flagship building for the UC San Diego campus. Construction began in 1968, and by September 1971, the new Central University Library was dedicated. Over the decades, the building has continued to evolve through expansions and renovations, adapting to the changing needs of the campus community. Tracing the history of the Library’s site design process, construction and expansion from 1965 to 1993, Shaping a Library draws on unique materials from UC San Diego Library’s Special Collections & Archives. From Pereira’s original spherical concept for Geisel Library to Gunnar Birkerts’ glass-walled expansion, architectural drawings, photographs and documents reveal the ideas, people and processes that shaped this beloved campus landmark. Shaping a Library is on view in the Exhibition Gallery on the 2nd (main) Floor of Geisel Library during the building's open hours from Saturday, September 26 through Tuesday, December 8, 2026. Can’t make it to campus to view the exhibition in-person? View the digital exhibit. Image Credit: Architectural rendering of UC San Diego Central University Library, William L. Pereira and Associates, 1965. UC San Diego Library, Special Collections & Archives.

title: The Human Condition: An Exploration of Art & Literature | Exhibit
description: The Human Condition: An Exploration of Art & Literature is an annual art and literary magazine created by medical students for the UC San Diego School of Medicine community. Now in its 32nd year, the student-led publication features art, photography, poetry, prose, sculpture, comics and more, providing a space for safe expression, creativity and exploring identities beyond medicine. This exhibition presents selected works from the 2025 and 2026 issues, offering a glimpse into the experiences, perspectives and creative lives of the School of Medicine community. Visitors are invited to pause, reflect and explore the many dimensions of the human experience. The Human Condition: An Exploration of Art & Literature is on view in the Sally T. WongAvery Library breezeway from September 26 to December 13, 2026, during the building's open hours. Previous issues of The Human Condition magazine, dating back to 2007-08, are available to download and read at your leisure. Curated by: Amy Xue, MS4, editor-in-chief, 2026-27 Myat Wai, MS4, editor-in-chief, 2026-27Supported by: UC San Diego School of MedicineUC San Diego Library

title: Library Milestones | Exhibit
description: Before the rise of digital publications and licensed electronic resources, academic libraries measured the size of their collections by the number of physical volumes on their shelves. Reaching a million-volume milestone was a source of pride and a mark of growth. This exhibit highlights five titles that mark milestones in the growth of the UC San Diego Library’s physical collections. Together, they also reflect the generosity of donors and support groups who helped build the collections and offer a glimpse into what made a book milestone-worthy at the time. Library Milestones is on view outside of Special Collections & Archives on the 2nd (main) Floor of Geisel Library during the building's open hours through Sunday, December 13, 2026. Photo citation: John Ogilby. America: being the latest, and most accurate description of the New World; containing the original inhabitants, and the remarkable voyages thither... title: Meteorites as Artistic Matter
description: Speakers: Ulrike Arnold , Artist; Gerard van Belle, PhD , Former Director of Science at Lowell Observatory; and Rachel Jans, PhD , Curator of Modern and Contemporary Art at The San Diego Museum of Art MOPA@SDMA Joan and Irwin Jacobs Theater Meteorites as Artistic Matter brings together internationally acclaimed artist Ulrike Arnold, astronomer Gerard van Belle, and the Museum’s Curator of Modern and Contemporary Art Rachel Jans, PhD, for a fascinating interdisciplinary conversation exploring the intersection of art, science, and the cosmos. Known for incorporating meteorite dust and pigments gathered from some of the world’s most remote landscapes into her paintings, Arnold will discuss how celestial and earthly materials become powerful artistic media. Joined by van Belle’s astronomical perspective and Jans’s expertise on the work of Sigmar Polke, a German artist also known for incorporating unconventional materials into his work, and contemporary artistic practice, this engaging guest lecture offers a rare opportunity to discover how meteorites inspire creativity, expand our understanding of materiality, and connect artistic expression with the vast universe beyond our planet. Following the lecture, guests are invited to enjoy a guided tour led by our docent team. Please note, this lecture is in-person only and held at the MOPA@SDMA Joan and Irwin Jacobs Theater in Balboa Park. $15 members and students | $20 seniors and military | $30 nonmembers This lecture is presented as a part of the Guest Lecture Series , which offers a platform for renowned scholars and experts from the art world to share their insights and knowledge on topics related to art history, art theory, and the museum’s collections.

title: Sacred Movement, Painted Prayers
description: Experience the intersection of living craft, tradition, and movement. Begin the evening with a performance of Nihon Buyo —Japanese classical dance—by acclaimed dancer Ichinosuke Umekawa. Formally trained in ballet and Kabuki theater, Umekawa brings folk narratives to life through fluid grace and masterful expression. Following the performance, join Guest Curator Meher McArthur to enjoy an advance preview of Painted Prayers — The Japanese Folk Art Tradition of Ema before the exhibition opens to the public the next day. McArthur will share her research and insights into these hand-painted wooden prayer tablets, illuminating the rich connections between sacred visual art, human devotion, and performing craft.

title: Bereza/Beryoze: Old Ukrainian and Yiddish songs in a new song cycle from Zozulka Trio
description: Many old songs brim with ecological awareness. Old songs from the territory of modern Ukraine tell stories about plants like the birch tree–bereza in Ukrainian, beryoze in Yiddish–that bend, break, and heal, becoming metaphors for human fragility and tenacity. Birds mark the turning of seasons and shifts in our internal weather as well. Since 2011, Zozulka–a trio named after the Ukrainian word for cuckoo bird–has interpreted songs from a wide range of Ukrainian village traditions. With BEREZA / BERYOZE, the trio branches into a new cycle of songs that speak directly to ecological themes. In this project, Zozulka reaches into Yiddish song repertoires from Ukraine, matching and contrasting the Jewish and Ukrainian song traditions that coexisted and drew upon grounded ecological knowledge. This song cycle reimagines old songs by rooting them in new sonic and cultural landscapes. Through expansive and bold arrangements, the works in BEREZA / BERYOZE illuminate how folk wisdom can deepen our awareness of the interdependence between human and more-than-human worlds. In an era marked by global climate change and devastating acts of ecocide in wartorn Ukraine and beyond, BEREZA / BERYOZE celebrates variegated and interlinked song traditions and the cathartic, regenerative power of singing old songs in the present. Performer Biography: Zozulka Trio is Eva Salina, Willa Roberts, and Maria Sonevytsky. We have been singing together since 2011, when we formed as an offshoot of The Chornobyl Songs Project, led by one of our mentors, the Kyiv-based ethnomusicologist Yevhen Yefremov. zozulka.bandcamp.com.

description: Candlelight Concerts are a series of original music concerts created by Fever aimed at democratizing access to culture by allowing people all over the world to enjoy live music candlelit performances played by local musicians in various stunning locations illuminated by thousands of candles. Candlelight was initially conceived as a classical music series with concerts featuring works from the greatest composers, such as Vivaldi, Mozart, and Chopin. Now, the ever-growing list of programs includes a wide variety of themes and genres, including tributes to contemporary like Queen, ABBA, Coldplay, and Ed Sheeran, as well as shows dedicated to K-Pop, movie soundtracks and many more. This multi-sensory experience has also evolved to feature different elements, such as ballet dancers or aerial performers, as well as other genres, such as jazz, soul, opera, flamenco, and more. Candlelight Concerts are present in more than 100 cities worldwide, with over 3 Million guests in attendance to date

title: Business Model Canvas 101
description: Whether you are a student startup with a brand new idea, a small business owner with a side project, or a seasoned business mogul, the Entrepreneur Workshops focus on a variety of topics pertinent to your journey. Sponsored by Pillsbury and hosted by the Office of Innovation and Commercialization’s The Basement, these workshops are open to everyone. We invite you to register for as many sessions as you are interested in! ​Event Description: ​Go back to basics and learn how successful founders turn complex ideas into clear, actionable strategies. In this interactive workshop, you will learn how to build your own Business Model Canvas, a fast, visual framework that organizes your entire venture into nine essential building blocks. ​Learn how to map your value proposition, customer segments, revenue streams, and key operations onto a single page. You’ll leave with a clear, flexible blueprint that helps you adapt quickly, align your team, and build a stronger startup with confidence. ​About the Speaker: ​Greg Horowitt | Director of Innovation Design, UC San Diego ​Greg Horowitt is Founding Partner of T2 Venture Creation and a co-author of ‘The Rainforest: The Secret to Building the Next Silicon Valley’. He presently serves as the Director of Innovation Design at the University of California, San Diego. He is a consultant to development organizations including the World Bank, OECD, USAID, Aspen Institute, and the National Academies of Science. In addition, he is a Kauffman Fellow and a Senior Fellow with the Global Federation of Competitiveness Councils. He previously served as an executive with a Berkshire Hathaway operating company for nearly twenty years

Drawing from conversations with adoptees, foster families, chosen families, and support networks, Roots of Loving Us examines how love, connection, and belonging shape our lives. Blending contemporary dance, storytelling, and multidisciplinary research, the work invites audiences to reflect on the many ways people create a sense of home. description: Do you have old magazines, vintage zines, or leftover craft supplies? We are gathering materials for a community Collage Poetry project that will be turned into a public exhibition. Collage Poetry weaves together existing text and visual fragments such as magazine cutouts, newspaper snippets, book jackets, zines, school reports/papers, and even non-paper materials (yarn, ribbon, glitter) to form a new, layered work of art. Check out examples from the Alice Notley Artworks collection, like Alone - I Pour a Cup or Vacuum. What to Donate: We are seeking materials in any language, including: Magazines and newspapersBook jackets and zinesOld school reports or papersMixed media (yarn, ribbon, fabric scraps, etc.)Where to Donate: Donations can be dropped off at the collection boxes located in the Service Hubs at Geisel Library and WongAvery Library during each building’s open hours. title: Shaping a Library | Exhibition
description: In early 1970, a San Diego newspaper announced, “Unique Library Taking Shape.” The headline referred to UC San Diego’s Central University Library, now Geisel Library, which was then under construction. The Library’s story began several years earlier. In 1965, architect William L. Pereira was invited to design the Central University Library, envisioned as the flagship building for the UC San Diego campus. Construction began in 1968, and by September 1971, the new Central University Library was dedicated. Over the decades, the building has continued to evolve through expansions and renovations, adapting to the changing needs of the campus community. Tracing the history of the Library’s site design process, construction and expansion from 1965 to 1993, Shaping a Library draws on unique materials from UC San Diego Library’s Special Collections & Archives. From Pereira’s original spherical concept for Geisel Library to Gunnar Birkerts’ glass-walled expansion, architectural drawings, photographs and documents reveal the ideas, people and processes that shaped this beloved campus landmark. Shaping a Library is on view in the Exhibition Gallery on the 2nd (main) Floor of Geisel Library during the building's open hours from Saturday, September 26 through Tuesday, December 8, 2026. Can’t make it to campus to view the exhibition in-person? View the digital exhibit. Image Credit: Architectural rendering of UC San Diego Central University Library, William L. Pereira and Associates, 1965. UC San Diego Library, Special Collections & Archives.

title: The Human Condition: An Exploration of Art & Literature | Exhibit
description: The Human Condition: An Exploration of Art & Literature is an annual art and literary magazine created by medical students for the UC San Diego School of Medicine community. Now in its 32nd year, the student-led publication features art, photography, poetry, prose, sculpture, comics and more, providing a space for safe expression, creativity and exploring identities beyond medicine. This exhibition presents selected works from the 2025 and 2026 issues, offering a glimpse into the experiences, perspectives and creative lives of the School of Medicine community. Visitors are invited to pause, reflect and explore the many dimensions of the human experience. The Human Condition: An Exploration of Art & Literature is on view in the Sally T. WongAvery Library breezeway from September 26 to December 13, 2026, during the building's open hours. Previous issues of The Human Condition magazine, dating back to 2007-08, are available to download and read at your leisure. Curated by: Amy Xue, MS4, editor-in-chief, 2026-27 Myat Wai, MS4, editor-in-chief, 2026-27Supported by: UC San Diego School of MedicineUC San Diego Library

title: Library Milestones | Exhibit
description: Before the rise of digital publications and licensed electronic resources, academic libraries measured the size of their collections by the number of physical volumes on their shelves. Reaching a million-volume milestone was a source of pride and a mark of growth. This exhibit highlights five titles that mark milestones in the growth of the UC San Diego Library’s physical collections. Together, they also reflect the generosity of donors and support groups who helped build the collections and offer a glimpse into what made a book milestone-worthy at the time. Library Milestones is on view outside of Special Collections & Archives on the 2nd (main) Floor of Geisel Library during the building's open hours through Sunday, December 13, 2026. Photo citation: John Ogilby. America: being the latest, and most accurate description of the New World; containing the original inhabitants, and the remarkable voyages thither... London: printed by the author, 1671. UC San Diego Library, Special Collections & Archives.

description: 2026 Fellowship Forum: New films. Big questions. Bold ideas. All are invited. Come meet the people shaping the future of cinematic arts. Each year, the Suraj Israni Center for Cinematic Arts offers fellowships to students, faculty, and staff across UC San Diego, providing funding and access to professional production equipment. Our fellows take the opportunity and run with it. They make films, experiment with new forms, conduct research, and build careers as artists and thinkers worth watching. The 2026 Fellowship Forum brings that work and the people behind it into focus. The afternoon event features three segments of project clips and brief panel conversations exploring the inspirations, challenges, and discoveries behind the work. title: Cancer Therapeutics Training (CT2) Seminar | Bodour Salhia, PhD
description: Cell-Free DNA Methylation Biomarkers in Cancer Care Dr. Bodour Salhia is the Inaugural Interim Chair of the Department of Cancer Biology and the Royce & Mary Trotter Chair in Cancer Research at the Keck School of Medicine of USC. She also co-leads the Epigenetic Regulation in Cancer (ERC) Program and serves as the Inaugural Director of the Preclinical Models Shared Resource at the USC Norris Comprehensive Cancer Center. A recognized leader in academic medicine, she is a fellow of the Hedwig van Ameringen Executive Leadership in Academic Medicine (ELAM) Program. A translational genomicist and epigenomicist, Dr. Salhia’s research integrates multi-omic technologies with functional and preclinical studies to address clinically urgent problems in cancer biology. Her work focuses on cfDNA methylation–based liquid biopsies for ovarian, breast, and colorectal cancer—efforts that have led to the development of OvaPrint™ for adnexal mass risk stratification and MammaTrace™ for minimal residual disease monitoring in breast cancer. She also leads the Eileen McGeever Breast Cancer Survivorship Program, advancing molecular approaches to recurrence risk prediction, and conducts research on the genomics and epigenomics of brain metastasis and degenerative eye disease. Her portfolio is supported by NIH, NSF, foundation, industry, and philanthropic funding. Motivated by the impact of liquid biopsy technologies on women’s health, she founded CpG Diagnostics, a USC spin-out dedicated to advancing cfDNA methylation diagnostics. Dr. Salhia is deeply committed to community engagement and patient-centered research. She founded The Bench with Bedside Initiative, a direct-to-patient research platform designed to bring scientists to patients and patients into the scientific process. Her outreach spans work with the Arizona Myeloma Network, The Wellness Community, Susan G. Komen, and underserved communities including the Navajo Nation. She has also traveled across Africa to support cancer education for scientists and clinicians. Her leadership and advocacy have earned numerous honors, including recognition as one of the “20 Faces of Komen,” Phoenix Business Journal’s Top 40 Under 40, community service awards from the Arizona Myeloma Network, and the 2024 USC Academic Senate Distinguished Faculty Service Award.

title: Shaping a Library | Exhibition
description: In early 1970, a San Diego newspaper announced, “Unique Library Taking Shape.” The headline referred to UC San Diego’s Central University Library, now Geisel Library, which was then under construction. The Library’s story began several years earlier. In 1965, architect William L. Pereira was invited to design the Central University Library, envisioned as the flagship building for the UC San Diego campus. Construction began in 1968, and by September 1971, the new Central University Library was dedicated. Over the decades, the building has continued to evolve through expansions and renovations, adapting to the changing needs of the campus community. Tracing the history of the Library’s site design process, construction and expansion from 1965 to 1993, Shaping a Library draws on unique materials from UC San Diego Library’s Special Collections & Archives. From Pereira’s original spherical concept for Geisel Library to Gunnar Birkerts’ glass-walled expansion, architectural drawings, photographs and documents reveal the ideas, people and processes that shaped this beloved campus landmark. Shaping a Library is on view in the Exhibition Gallery on the 2nd (main) Floor of Geisel Library during the building's open hours from Saturday, September 26 through Tuesday, December 8, 2026. Can’t make it to campus to view the exhibition in-person? View the digital exhibit. Image Credit: Architectural rendering of UC San Diego Central University Library, William L. Pereira and Associates, 1965. UC San Diego Library, Special Collections & Archives.

title: Between Political Liberalism and Dictatorship: Military Intervention and the Crisis of Hegemony in Interwar Greece
venue: Ida and Cecil Green Faculty Club
description: This talk examines the crisis of political liberalism in interwar Greece by analyzing the recurrent intervention of the military in politics as a structural consequence of the failure to establish a durable bourgeois hegemony after 1916, with particular emphasis on the Second Hellenic Republic (1924–1935). It argues that the frequent military interventions in the political scene of the period were not an episodic disruption of an otherwise functioning parliamentary order, but rather conceptualizes the army as a structural political actor within a fragile liberal regime. Speaker Bio: George Souvlis completed his PhD at the European University Institute (Department of History and Civilization) in Florence. He has taught courses in modern and contemporary Greek and European history and sociology at Democritus University of Thrace (2019–2020) and the University of Ioannina (2020–2023). Since 2025, he has been a researcher in the ERC Starting Grant project STEXEU — The Constitutional Road to Dictatorship: States of Exception and Authoritarianism in Europe, 1900–1939, coordinated by Arturo Zoffmann Rodríguez at the Institute of Contemporary History (IHC), NOVA University Lisbon, and funded by the European Research Council (ERC Starting Grant, Grant Agreement No. 101163723). His research interests lie in the fields of fascist studies, intellectual history, and historical sociology. His most recent publications include the books and edited volumes Voices on the Left (2019), Back to the ’30s? Crisis, Repetition, and Transition in the 20th and 21st Centuries (co-edited with J. Rayner, S. Falls, and T. Nelms, 2020), The Normalization of Far-Right Discourse in Greece (co-edited with R. Vasilaki, 2021), the special issue Re-assessing the Metaxas Dictatorship (1936–1941): Greek Fascism or Old-Style Authoritarianism? (Fascism, 11(2), 2022; co-edited with A. Kallis), Radical Journalism (co-edited with S. Farrell and E. Siapera, 2023), Duty to Revolt: Transnational and Commemorative Aspects of Revolution (co-edited with A. Karatzogianni, 2023), The Alternative Right in Greece (2025), and Politics of Liberation: Conversations with Theory and History (co-edited with R. Vasilaki, 2025). He has also published articles in journals including Praksis, Journal of Contemporary Central and Eastern Europe, Fascism: Journal of Comparative Fascist Studies, Práticas da História, and Critical Education. Hosted By: Center for Hellenic Studies Program

title: Leading with Purpose
description: Whether you are a student startup with a brand new idea, a small business owner with a side project, or a seasoned business mogul, the Entrepreneur Workshops focus on a variety of topics pertinent to your journey. Sponsored by Pillsbury and hosted by the Office of Innovation and Commercialization’s The Basement, these workshops are open to everyone. We invite you to register for as many sessions as you are interested in! ​Event Description: ​Are you defining your worth by your grades, startup, or next internship offer? In an achievement-obsessed culture, it’s easy to confuse what you do with who you are. ​This interactive session flips the script on traditional success to explore how our definitions of joy and fulfillment directly shape the quality of our lives. Through hands-on activities like the Core Values Exercise, you will pinpoint what actually drives you, align your daily decisions with your values, trade blame for personal accountability, and build authentic connections with others. ​Whether you are launching a business, preparing for graduation, or simply navigating UC San Diego, this workshop will give you the clarity to lead yourself and others through a lens of purpose rather than accomplishment while coming from a place of peace rather than stress. ​ ​This workshop is part of the iLead program. Attend this workshop to earn points towards your Leadership Certificate and CCR validation.

title: Collage Poetry Exhibition Donation Drive
description: Do you have old magazines, vintage zines, or leftover craft supplies? We are gathering materials for a community Collage Poetry project that will be turned into a public exhibition. What is Collage Poetry? Collage Poetry weaves together existing text and visual fragments such as magazine cutouts, newspaper snippets, book jackets, zines, school reports/papers, and even non-paper materials (yarn, ribbon, glitter) to form a new, layered work of art. Check out examples from the Alice Notley Artworks collection, like Alone - I Pour a Cup or Vacuum. What to Donate: We are seeking materials in any language, including: Magazines and newspapersBook jackets and zinesOld school reports or papersMixed media (yarn, ribbon, fabric scraps, etc.)Where to Donate: Donations can be dropped off at the collection boxes located in the Service Hubs at Geisel Library and WongAvery Library during each building’s open hours. View Geisel’s hoursView WongAvery’s hours (note: WongAvery is closed on Saturdays)Note: All donations are final and will not be returned. Please ensure all donated papers, reports, or documents are free of sensitive or personal information. We kindly ask that all donations be clean and free of mold, odors, or pests. For safety reasons, please do not donate hazardous materials, including broken glass, chemicals, or sharp metal objects. Questions? Contact us at ucsdlibrary@ucsd.edu.

title: Shaping a Library | Exhibition
description: In early 1970, a San Diego newspaper announced, “Unique Library Taking Shape.” The headline referred to UC San Diego’s Central University Library, now Geisel Library, which was then under construction. The Library’s story began several years earlier. In 1965, architect William L. Pereira was invited to design the Central University Library, envisioned as the flagship building for the UC San Diego campus. Construction began in 1968, and by September 1971, the new Central University Library was dedicated. Over the decades, the building has continued to evolve through expansions and renovations, adapting to the changing needs of the campus community. Tracing the history of the Library’s site design process, construction and expansion from 1965 to 1993, Shaping a Library draws on unique materials from UC San Diego Library’s Special Collections & Archives. From Pereira’s original spherical concept for Geisel Library to Gunnar Birkerts’ glass-walled expansion, architectural drawings, photographs and documents reveal the ideas, people and processes that shaped this beloved campus landmark. Shaping a Library is on view in the Exhibition Gallery on the 2nd (main) Floor of Geisel Library during the building's open hours from Saturday, September 26 through Tuesday, December 8, 2026. Can’t make it to campus to view the exhibition in-person? View the digital exhibit. Image Credit: Architectural rendering of UC San Diego Central University Library, William L. Pereira and Associates, 1965. UC San Diego Library, Special Collections & Archives.

title: The Human Condition: An Exploration of Art & Literature | Exhibit
description: The Human Condition: An Exploration of Art & Literature is an annual art and literary magazine created by medical students for the UC San Diego School of Medicine community. Now in its 32nd year, the student-led publication features art, photography, poetry, prose, sculpture, comics and more, providing a space for safe expression, creativity and exploring identities beyond medicine. This exhibition presents selected works from the 2025 and 2026 issues, offering a glimpse into the experiences, perspectives and creative lives of the School of Medicine community. Visitors are invited to pause, reflect and explore the many dimensions of the human experience. The Human Condition: An Exploration of Art & Literature is on view in the Sally T. WongAvery Library breezeway from September 26 to December 13, 2026, during the building's open hours. Previous issues of The Human Condition magazine, dating back to 2007-08, are available to download and read at your leisure. Curated by: Amy Xue, MS4, editor-in-chief, 2026-27 Myat Wai, MS4, editor-in-chief, 2026-27Supported by: UC San Diego School of MedicineUC San Diego Library

title: Library Milestones | Exhibit
description: Before the rise of digital publications and licensed electronic resources, academic libraries measured the size of their collections by the number of physical volumes on their shelves. Reaching a million-volume milestone was a source of pride and a mark of growth. This exhibit highlights five titles that mark milestones in the growth of the UC San Diego Library’s physical collections. Together, they also reflect the generosity of donors and support groups who helped build the collections and offer a glimpse into what made a book milestone-worthy at the time. Library Milestones is on view outside of Special Collections & Archives on the 2nd (main) Floor of Geisel Library during the building's open hours through Sunday, December 13, 2026. Photo citation: John Ogilby. America: being the latest, and most accurate description of the New World; containing the original inhabitants, and the remarkable voyages thither... London: printed by the author, 1671. UC San Diego Library, Special Collections & Archives.

title: Volcanoes: The Fires of Creation
description: Volcanoes have helped create our world. The continents, the air we breathe and even life itself have their origins in fire. These processes have created extraordinary ecosystems and wildlife habitats. The story of volcanoes is the story of the planet’s creation and the story of us. Volcanoes: The Fires of Creation , lets you witness the 2018 Kilauea eruption in Hawaii; see the archaeological remains of Pompeii, devastated almost 2,000 years ago by Mount Vesuvius; visit Mount Fuji in Japan, made up of three volcanoes—Fuji on top and two others hidden beneath; and marvel at the black molten lava of Ol Doinyo Lengai in Tanzania.

title: Anne Frank: Her World and Ours, Featuring Ruth Franklin
description: Ruth Franklin, author of “The Many Lives of Anne Frank” (2025), will discuss some lesser-known aspects of the diary’s creation and reception as well as the urgency of Anne Frank’s story in our current moment. Last January, as videos of violence by ICE agents made international headlines, Minnesota Governor Tim Walz noted the similarities between the raids on immigrants and “that story of Anne Frank.” Meanwhile, antisemitism is on the rise around the world, including in Amsterdam, Anne’s adopted home. Can Anne’s story still speak to the experience of persecuted Jews even as it becomes a metaphor for racism and xenophobia of all kinds? How to Attend / Submit a Question Because Ruth Franklin will be joining us from Europe, this program will be prerecorded and released on YouTube at 5 p.m. Pacific time on Thursday, October 22. A link to the recording will be added to this event listing when it is available. We invite you to submit a question for Ruth prior to the recording. Submit your question by 4 p.m. Pacific time on Wednesday, October 14. We'll do our best to address as many questions as possible during the program, though we cannot guarantee that every question will be answered. About the Speaker Ruth Franklin is a renowned book critic and former editor at The New Republic whose writing has appeared in major publications including The New Yorker, The New York Times Book Review, and Harper's. Her acclaimed 2016 biography, “Shirley Jackson: A Rather Haunted Life,” won the National Book Critics Circle Award and was widely named one of the year's best books by outlets such as The New York Times, Time magazine, and NPR. She is also the author of “A Thousand Darknesses: Lies and Truth in Holocaust Fiction,” which was named a finalist for the Sami Rohr Prize for Jewish Literature. Franklin has been recognized with prestigious fellowships from the Guggenheim Foundation, the Cullman Center and the Leon Levy Center. About the Series The Holocaust Living History Workshop (HLHW) series is an education and outreach program co-sponsored by the UC San Diego Library and the Jewish Studies Program. It aims to preserve the memories of the victims and survivors of the Holocaust by offering public events involving witnesses, descendants and scholars and through the use of the USC Shoah Foundation Institute’s Visual History Archive. Past HLHW workshops are now part of the Library’s digital collections and are available online.

title: 2026 Nierenberg Prize for Science in the Public Interest
description: As a young girl, France A. Córdova was inspired by the night sky-its immensity, its mysteries, and our fragile place within it. That wonder led her to a career as an astrophysicist and to leadership roles at NASA, the National Science Foundation, and major research universities. Today, Córdova looks upward with growing concern. Just as we have altered Earth's environment, we are beginning to transform the space environment. Satellite mega-constellations are increasing orbital congestion and creating optical and radio interference that threaten humanity's ability to observe and understand the universe. Córdova’s presentation, “Vanishing Darkness: Preserving Our Window to the Universe,” will explore how we can balance technological innovation with stewardship. Preserving an unobstructed window on the universe is not about resisting progress; it is about ensuring that humanity's expanding presence in space enhances, rather than diminishes, our capacity for discovery. Learn more about Córdova and her career. Seating is limited and registration is required for this event. Those interested in attending should RSVP in advance.

description: Do you have old magazines, vintage zines, or leftover craft supplies? We are gathering materials for a community Collage Poetry project that will be turned into a public exhibition. Collage Poetry weaves together existing text and visual fragments such as magazine cutouts, newspaper snippets, book jackets, zines, school reports/papers, and even non-paper materials (yarn, ribbon, glitter) to form a new, layered work of art. Check out examples from the Alice Notley Artworks collection, like Alone - I Pour a Cup or Vacuum. View Geisel’s hoursView WongAvery’s hours (note: WongAvery is closed on Saturdays)Note: All donations are final and will not be returned. For safety reasons, please do not donate hazardous materials, including broken glass, chemicals, or sharp metal objects. Questions? Contact us at ucsdlibrary@ucsd.edu.

title: Shaping a Library | Exhibition
description: In early 1970, a San Diego newspaper announced, “Unique Library Taking Shape.” The headline referred to UC San Diego’s Central University Library, now Geisel Library, which was then under construction. The Library’s story began several years earlier. In 1965, architect William L. Pereira was invited to design the Central University Library, envisioned as the flagship building for the UC San Diego campus. Construction began in 1968, and by September 1971, the new Central University Library was dedicated. Over the decades, the building has continued to evolve through expansions and renovations, adapting to the changing needs of the campus community. Tracing the history of the Library’s site design process, construction and expansion from 1965 to 1993, Shaping a Library draws on unique materials from UC San Diego Library’s Special Collections & Archives. From Pereira’s original spherical concept for Geisel Library to Gunnar Birkerts’ glass-walled expansion, architectural drawings, photographs and documents reveal the ideas, people and processes that shaped this beloved campus landmark. Shaping a Library is on view in the Exhibition Gallery on the 2nd (main) Floor of Geisel Library during the building's open hours from Saturday, September 26 through Tuesday, December 8, 2026. Can’t make it to campus to view the exhibition in-person? View the digital exhibit. Image Credit: Architectural rendering of UC San Diego Central University Library, William L. Pereira and Associates, 1965. UC San Diego Library, Special Collections & Archives.

title: The Human Condition: An Exploration of Art & Literature | Exhibit
description: The Human Condition: An Exploration of Art & Literature is an annual art and literary magazine created by medical students for the UC San Diego School of Medicine community. Now in its 32nd year, the student-led publication features art, photography, poetry, prose, sculpture, comics and more, providing a space for safe expression, creativity and exploring identities beyond medicine. This exhibition presents selected works from the 2025 and 2026 issues, offering a glimpse into the experiences, perspectives and creative lives of the School of Medicine community. Visitors are invited to pause, reflect and explore the many dimensions of the human experience. The Human Condition: An Exploration of Art & Literature is on view in the Sally T. WongAvery Library breezeway from September 26 to December 13, 2026, during the building's open hours. Previous issues of The Human Condition magazine, dating back to 2007-08, are available to download and read at your leisure. Curated by: Amy Xue, MS4, editor-in-chief, 2026-27 Myat Wai, MS4, editor-in-chief, 2026-27Supported by: UC San Diego School of MedicineUC San Diego Library

title: Library Milestones | Exhibit
description: Before the rise of digital publications and licensed electronic resources, academic libraries measured the size of their collections by the number of physical volumes on their shelves. Reaching a million-volume milestone was a source of pride and a mark of growth. This exhibit highlights five titles that mark milestones in the growth of the UC San Diego Library’s physical collections. Together, they also reflect the generosity of donors and support groups who helped build the collections and offer a glimpse into what made a book milestone-worthy at the time. Library Milestones is on view outside of Special Collections & Archives on the 2nd (main) Floor of Geisel Library during the building's open hours through Sunday, December 13, 2026. Photo citation: John Ogilby. America: being the latest, and most accurate description of the New World; containing the original inhabitants, and the remarkable voyages thither... London: printed by the author, 1671. UC San Diego Library, Special Collections & Archives.

title: Painted Prayers: Japanese Ema Votive Plaques
description: Ema (literally, “picture horse”) are wooden votive plaques on which visitors to Shinto shrines and Buddhist temples have for centuries written their prayers and wishes for the _kami _or Buddhist deities to read. Though these plaques originally featured horses, they evolved to feature many different images associated with various wishes, from good fortune to health to love and relationships. In conjunction with the exhibition Painted Prayers: The Japanese Folk Art Tradition of Ema , exhibition curator and Japanese art historian, Meher McArthur will explore the history of these votive plaques, the meanings behind some of the images, and their role in contemporary Japanese spiritual culture.

title: Wander the Wetlands - Work Party
description: Join UC San Diego Natural Reserve System and San Diego Bird Alliance every 2nd and 4th Saturday of the month from 9-11am for Wander the Wetlands! Wander the Wetlands is a chance for any and everyone to learn more about the history of the marsh, the unique habitats it holds, and the animals that call the Kendall-Frost Marsh home. No RSVP or registration needed. Each 4th Saturday event is a dedicated work party! Meet us at the Kendall-Frost Marsh Field Station and Community Learning Center. title: Shaping a Library | Exhibition
description: In early 1970, a San Diego newspaper announced, “Unique Library Taking Shape.” The headline referred to UC San Diego’s Central University Library, now Geisel Library, which was then under construction. The Library’s story began several years earlier. In 1965, architect William L. Pereira was invited to design the Central University Library, envisioned as the flagship building for the UC San Diego campus. Construction began in 1968, and by September 1971, the new Central University Library was dedicated. Over the decades, the building has continued to evolve through expansions and renovations, adapting to the changing needs of the campus community. Tracing the history of the Library’s site design process, construction and expansion from 1965 to 1993, Shaping a Library draws on unique materials from UC San Diego Library’s Special Collections & Archives. From Pereira’s original spherical concept for Geisel Library to Gunnar Birkerts’ glass-walled expansion, architectural drawings, photographs and documents reveal the ideas, people and processes that shaped this beloved campus landmark. Shaping a Library is on view in the Exhibition Gallery on the 2nd (main) Floor of Geisel Library during the building's open hours from Saturday, September 26 through Tuesday, December 8, 2026. Can’t make it to campus to view the exhibition in-person? View the digital exhibit. Image Credit: Architectural rendering of UC San Diego Central University Library, William L. Pereira and Associates, 1965. UC San Diego Library, Special Collections & Archives.

title: The Human Condition: An Exploration of Art & Literature | Exhibit

Now in its 32nd year, the student-led publication features art, photography, poetry, prose, sculpture, comics and more, providing a space for safe expression, creativity and exploring identities beyond medicine. This exhibition presents selected works from the 2025 and 2026 issues, offering a glimpse into the experiences, perspectives and creative lives of the School of Medicine community. Visitors are invited to pause, reflect and explore the many dimensions of the human experience. The Human Condition: An Exploration of Art & Literature is on view in the Sally T. WongAvery Library breezeway from September 26 to December 13, 2026, during the building's open hours. Previous issues of The Human Condition magazine, dating back to 2007-08, are available to download and read at your leisure. Curated by: Amy Xue, MS4, editor-in-chief, 2026-27 Myat Wai, MS4, editor-in-chief, 2026-27Supported by: UC San Diego School of MedicineUC San Diego Library

title: Library Milestones | Exhibit

title: Koto Lessons
address: 2215 Pan American Road East, San Diego, CA, 92101
description: Koto, also called kin, long Japanese board zither having 13 silk strings and movable bridges. The body of the instrument is made of paulownia wood and is about 190 cm (74 inches) long. When the performer is kneeling or seated on the floor, the koto is held off the floor by two legs or a bridge-storage box; in most modern concerts, the instrument is placed on a stand so the performer can sit on a chair. The koto is played by plucking the strings with the thumb and first two fingers of the right hand, which are fitted with ivory plectrums called tsume. The left hand, in traditions after the 16th century, may alter the pitch or sound of each string by pressing or manipulating the strings to the left of the bridges. Various pentatonic tunings are used, depending on the type of music being played. The koto appeared in the Japanese court during the 8th century and was called the gakusō. Schools for the bourgeois were established in the 16th century. Two of these—Ikuta (started in the 17th century) and Yamada (opened in the 18th century)—continue to the present day. Solo (danmono) and chamber (sankyoku) music dominate the repertory, and in the latter form the koto player often sings as well. title: Art in the Evening: The Moods of Early Russian Art
description: Join us for a special Art in the Evening program featuring Justin Willson, Curator at The Icon Museum and Study Center in Clinton, Massachusetts, as he illuminates one of the most transformative periods in Russian icon painting. Drawing upon exceptional works in the Timken collection, Willson will trace developments in style and patronage across fifteenth- and sixteenth-century Muscovy, beginning with painters in the circle of Dionisiy and revealing how a sweeping religious revival reshaped the artistic and spiritual character of early Russian art. Set against the intimate backdrop of the Museum’s galleries, the evening offers a rare opportunity to experience the Timken’s distinguished collection of Russian icons through the perspective of a leading scholar in the field. Guests are invited to enjoy wine and curated nibbles before the lecture, followed by an engaging conversation that brings new insight to works whose beauty and spiritual resonance have endured for centuries. The lecture coincides with the release of Wilson’s book, The Moods of Early Russian Art (University of Chicago Press, 2026). Copies of the book will be available for purchase at the event.

description: Join award-winning Chef Spencer Hunter of Lia’s Lumpia on October 25, 2026, from 6:00–8:00 PM at the San Diego History Center for a Kamayan feast celebrating Filipino American History Month. A San Diego native and finalist on Food Network’s Great Food Truck Race, Chef Spencer honors his Filipino grandmother’s culinary legacy while blending it with his African American roots. He has taken first place for his Sisig Lumpia, cheffed for distinguished clientele ranging from corporate leaders to members of the British Royal Family, and continues to redefine what modern fusion cuisine can be. Kamayan is a traditional Filipino style of communal dining where food is spread across a table lined with fresh banana leaves and shared by everyone. SDHC’s Kamayan feast will feature: Appetizers: Bacon Jalapeño Popper Lumpia Filipino Cheese and Charcuterie Grazing Table Feast: Mango Mixed Greens Salad (plated at each seat) Sinigang Pork Bone Broth (plated at each seat) JUMBO Lola’s Pork LUMPIA Calamansi Chicken Wings Classic Chicken Adobo Bangus (Milkfish) Sisig Braised Beef & Potatoes Bistec Steamed Jasmine Rice Vegetable Pancit Noodles Pickled Cucumbers & Cherry Tomatoes Sweet Chili Sauce, Garlic Vinegar, Sriracha, Soy Sauce Freshly sliced fruit Sweet Bites: Guava Cream Cheese LUMPIA Tickets include appetizers, kamayan feast, complimentary beverages, and after-hours admission to SDHC exhibits, including Taste San Diego: Filipino Culinary Journeys. title: Art + Design Workshop: Floral Arranging
description: Celebrate the beauty and abundance of the season with a morning of floral design at the Timken. Inspired by the rich colors, textures, and graceful compositions found in the Museum’s collection, this hands-on workshop invites participants to create an elegant autumn arrangement using a thoughtfully selected palette of seasonal flowers and foliage. Under the guidance of a professional floral designer, participants will explore the principles of balance, color, form, and movement that unite the traditions of painting and floral design. Each guest will create a distinctive arrangement to take home. No prior floral design experience is necessary. Workshop fee includes all materials, tools, and light refreshments. About the Artist: Anne Latham is a floral designer, photographer, ceramicist, garden designer, and artist. As the principal designer of Three Swords Floral Co., she leads an exceptional team of designers, traveling around California and Hawai’i to craft floral experiences for private estates, destination weddings, and discreet brand activations. Anne has been flowering since 2015, following her formal training as a bookbinder and lithographer at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. Her Midwestern roots and background as an artist, studio assistant, and time spent in the hospitality industry continue to inform her refined, grounded, and deeply personal approach to floral design.

title: Securing the Future: U.S.-Korea Cooperation in Defense, AI and Trade
description: Securing the Future: U.S.-Korea Cooperation in Defense, AI and Trade examines how the United States and the Republic of Korea are navigating critical shifts in economic and national security. As geopolitical competition accelerates, aligning strategic industrial policies and defense capabilities is essential to building enduring alliance resilience. This public roundtable brings together top policy, industry and defense leaders to unpack three interconnected fronts: the strategic landscape of artificial intelligence (AI), the impact of maritime trade policy and the Jones Act on shipbuilding and logistics, and evolving security dynamics in the Indo-Pacific. This public lecture series is organized by the Korea-Pacific Program at the UC San Diego School of Global Policy and Strategy (GPS). For more information on program activities, please visit gps.ucsd.edu/kpp. If you have any questions, please contact GPS Events Coordinator Susan Zau.

title: Collage Poetry Exhibition Donation Drive
description: Do you have old magazines, vintage zines, or leftover craft supplies? We are gathering materials for a community Collage Poetry project that will be turned into a public exhibition. What is Collage Poetry? Collage Poetry weaves together existing text and visual fragments such as magazine cutouts, newspaper snippets, book jackets, zines, school reports/papers, and even non-paper materials (yarn, ribbon, glitter) to form a new, layered work of art. Check out examples from the Alice Notley Artworks collection, like Alone - I Pour a Cup or Vacuum. What to Donate: We are seeking materials in any language, including: Magazines and newspapersBook jackets and zinesOld school reports or papersMixed media (yarn, ribbon, fabric scraps, etc.)Where to Donate: Donations can be dropped off at the collection boxes located in the Service Hubs at Geisel Library and WongAvery Library during each building’s open hours. View Geisel’s hoursView WongAvery’s hours (note: WongAvery is closed on Saturdays)Note: All donations are final and will not be returned. Please ensure all donated papers, reports, or documents are free of sensitive or personal information. We kindly ask that all donations be clean and free of mold, odors, or pests. For safety reasons, please do not donate hazardous materials, including broken glass, chemicals, or sharp metal objects. Questions? Contact us at ucsdlibrary@ucsd.edu.

title: Shaping a Library | Exhibition
description: In early 1970, a San Diego newspaper announced, “Unique Library Taking Shape.” The headline referred to UC San Diego’s Central University Library, now Geisel Library, which was then under construction. The Library’s story began several years earlier. In 1965, architect William L. Pereira was invited to design the Central University Library, envisioned as the flagship building for the UC San Diego campus. Construction began in 1968, and by September 1971, the new Central University Library was dedicated. Over the decades, the building has continued to evolve through expansions and renovations, adapting to the changing needs of the campus community. Tracing the history of the Library’s site design process, construction and expansion from 1965 to 1993, Shaping a Library draws on unique materials from UC San Diego Library’s Special Collections & Archives. From Pereira’s original spherical concept for Geisel Library to Gunnar Birkerts’ glass-walled expansion, architectural drawings, photographs and documents reveal the ideas, people and processes that shaped this beloved campus landmark. Shaping a Library is on view in the Exhibition Gallery on the 2nd (main) Floor of Geisel Library during the building's open hours from Saturday, September 26 through Tuesday, December 8, 2026. Can’t make it to campus to view the exhibition in-person? View the digital exhibit. Image Credit: Architectural rendering of UC San Diego Central University Library, William L. Pereira and Associates, 1965. UC San Diego Library, Special Collections & Archives.

title: The Human Condition: An Exploration of Art & Literature | Exhibit
description: The Human Condition: An Exploration of Art & Literature is an annual art and literary magazine created by medical students for the UC San Diego School of Medicine community. Now in its 32nd year, the student-led publication features art, photography, poetry, prose, sculpture, comics and more, providing a space for safe expression, creativity and exploring identities beyond medicine. This exhibition presents selected works from the 2025 and 2026 issues, offering a glimpse into the experiences, perspectives and creative lives of the School of Medicine community. Visitors are invited to pause, reflect and explore the many dimensions of the human experience. The Human Condition: An Exploration of Art & Literature is on view in the Sally T. WongAvery Library breezeway from September 26 to December 13, 2026, during the building's open hours. Previous issues of The Human Condition magazine, dating back to 2007-08, are available to download and read at your leisure. Curated by: Amy Xue, MS4, editor-in-chief, 2026-27 Myat Wai, MS4, editor-in-chief, 2026-27Supported by: UC San Diego School of MedicineUC San Diego Library

title: Library Milestones | Exhibit
description: Before the rise of digital publications and licensed electronic resources, academic libraries measured the size of their collections by the number of physical volumes on their shelves. Reaching a million-volume milestone was a source of pride and a mark of growth. Together, they also reflect the generosity of donors and support groups who helped build the collections and offer a glimpse into what made a book milestone-worthy at the time. Library Milestones is on view outside of Special Collections & Archives on the 2nd (main) Floor of Geisel Library during the building's open hours through Sunday, December 13, 2026. London: printed by the author, 1671. UC San Diego Library, Special Collections & Archives.

title: WEDS@7 Mark Dresser "Gradience Quartet"
venue: Conrad Prebys Music Center Experimental Theater
description: Following their stunning world premiere at The Stone in NYC in September 2025, Mark Dresser’s Gradience Quartet makes its highly anticipated debut at UC San Diego. Bringing together a strikingly unconventional instrumentation, the ensemble fluidly blurs the boundaries of genre and traditional musical parameters. Yet, beyond the structural innovation of their compositions, the defining force of this quartet is their profound emotional and improvisational synergy. Their performance promises a rare, captivating chemistry where distinct sonic worlds merge with breathtaking intimacy and power. Gradience Quartet: Mark Dresser – acoustic bass DoYeon Kim – gayageum, vocals Cory Smythe – electro acoustic piano Sara Schoenbeck – bassoon Mark Dresser is a Grammy nominated, internationally renowned bass player, improviser, and composer. At the core of his music is an obsession and commitment to expanding the sonic, musical, and expressive possibilities of the contrabass. He has recorded over one hundred-fifty CDs including ten CDs as composer/bandleader, seven solo recordings and a DVD. His solo recording, “Tines of Change” was listed in the “Best Recordings of 2023” by Downbeat Magazine. His latest, solo recording In the Shadow of A Mad King features a duo with the late great poet Jerome Rothenberg, (Tzadik 2024).

Check out examples from the Alice Notley Artworks collection, like Alone - I Pour a Cup or Vacuum. What to Donate: We are seeking materials in any language, including: Magazines and newspapersBook jackets and zinesOld school reports or papersMixed media (yarn, ribbon, fabric scraps, etc.)Where to Donate: Donations can be dropped off at the collection boxes located in the Service Hubs at Geisel Library and WongAvery Library during each building’s open hours. View Geisel’s hoursView WongAvery’s hours (note: WongAvery is closed on Saturdays)Note: All donations are final and will not be returned. Please ensure all donated papers, reports, or documents are free of sensitive or personal information. We kindly ask that all donations be clean and free of mold, odors, or pests. For safety reasons, please do not donate hazardous materials, including broken glass, chemicals, or sharp metal objects. Questions? Contact us at ucsdlibrary@ucsd.edu.

title: Shaping a Library | Exhibition
description: In early 1970, a San Diego newspaper announced, “Unique Library Taking Shape.” The headline referred to UC San Diego’s Central University Library, now Geisel Library, which was then under construction. The Library’s story began several years earlier. In 1965, architect William L. Pereira was invited to design the Central University Library, envisioned as the flagship building for the UC San Diego campus. Construction began in 1968, and by September 1971, the new Central University Library was dedicated. Over the decades, the building has continued to evolve through expansions and renovations, adapting to the changing needs of the campus community. Tracing the history of the Library’s site design process, construction and expansion from 1965 to 1993, Shaping a Library draws on unique materials from UC San Diego Library’s Special Collections & Archives. From Pereira’s original spherical concept for Geisel Library to Gunnar Birkerts’ glass-walled expansion, architectural drawings, photographs and documents reveal the ideas, people and processes that shaped this beloved campus landmark. Shaping a Library is on view in the Exhibition Gallery on the 2nd (main) Floor of Geisel Library during the building's open hours from Saturday, September 26 through Tuesday, December 8, 2026. Can’t make it to campus to view the exhibition in-person? View the digital exhibit. Image Credit: Architectural rendering of UC San Diego Central University Library, William L. Pereira and Associates, 1965. UC San Diego Library, Special Collections & Archives.

title: We Are What We Ate: The Diets that Fueled Human Evolution
description: Join CARTA in-person at the Salk Institute or online on Friday, October 30, for our free public symposium, We Are What We Ate: The Diets that Fueled Human Evolution! For more information and to register to attend, please visit https://carta.anthropogeny.org/events/we-are-what-we-ate-diets-fueled-human-evolution ABSTRACT: The vast majority of human evolutionary history was fueled by diets composed exclusively of wild foods gathered and hunted rather than planted and raised. Compared to our ape-ancestors, and in contrast to today's living apes, members of the genus Homo have increasingly relied on technology and cumulative culture, such as use of complex tools, fire, and later fermentation, to access a broader range of foods across diverse ecosystems while defining foodways and regional identities. These innovations facilitated the global radiation of humans to every corner of the planet. Following the Last Glacial Maximum, approximately 12,000 years ago, the transition to agriculture marked a pivotal shift in human dietary patterns. The domestication of crops and livestock enabled food surplus, sedentism, and population growth, while introducing new nutritional and health consequences. More recently, widespread industrial food processing and ultra-refined diets may be driving additional physiological changes with unknown consequences for metabolism, disease, and the human microbiome, along with environmental impacts. This symposium examines the diets that fueled human evolution, drawing on evidence from paleontology, archeology, genetics, comparative anatomy and physiology, modern nutritional science, microbiome research, and ethnographic studies of the few remaining living foragers. Together, these perspectives can illuminate how dietary adaptations have shaped and continue to influence human biology, health, and culture.

title: Collage Poetry Exhibition Donation Drive
description: Do you have old magazines, vintage zines, or leftover craft supplies? We are gathering materials for a community Collage Poetry project that will be turned into a public exhibition. What is Collage Poetry? Collage Poetry weaves together existing text and visual fragments such as magazine cutouts, newspaper snippets, book jackets, zines, school reports/papers, and even non-paper materials (yarn, ribbon, glitter) to form a new, layered work of art. Check out examples from the Alice Notley Artworks collection, like Alone - I Pour a Cup or Vacuum. What to Donate: We are seeking materials in any language, including: Magazines and newspapersBook jackets and zinesOld school reports or papersMixed media (yarn, ribbon, fabric scraps, etc.)Where to Donate: Donations can be dropped off at the collection boxes located in the Service Hubs at Geisel Library and WongAvery Library during each building’s open hours. View Geisel’s hoursView WongAvery’s hours (note: WongAvery is closed on Saturdays)Note: All donations are final and will not be returned. Please ensure all donated papers, reports, or documents are free of sensitive or personal information. We kindly ask that all donations be clean and free of mold, odors, or pests. For safety reasons, please do not donate hazardous materials, including broken glass, chemicals, or sharp metal objects. Questions? Contact us at ucsdlibrary@ucsd.edu.

title: Shaping a Library | Exhibition
description: In early 1970, a San Diego newspaper announced, “Unique Library Taking Shape.” The headline referred to UC San Diego’s Central University Library, now Geisel Library, which was then under construction. The Library’s story began several years earlier. In 1965, architect William L. Pereira was invited to design the Central University Library, envisioned as the flagship building for the UC San Diego campus. Construction began in 1968, and by September 1971, the new Central University Library was dedicated. Over the decades, the building has continued to evolve through expansions and renovations, adapting to the changing needs of the campus community. Tracing the history of the Library’s site design process, construction and expansion from 1965 to 1993, Shaping a Library draws on unique materials from UC San Diego Library’s Special Collections & Archives. From Pereira’s original spherical concept for Geisel Library to Gunnar Birkerts’ glass-walled expansion, architectural drawings, photographs and documents reveal the ideas, people and processes that shaped this beloved campus landmark. Shaping a Library is on view in the Exhibition Gallery on the 2nd (main) Floor of Geisel Library during the building's open hours from Saturday, September 26 through Tuesday, December 8, 2026. Can’t make it to campus to view the exhibition in-person? View the digital exhibit. Image Credit: Architectural rendering of UC San Diego Central University Library, William L. Pereira and Associates, 1965. UC San Diego Library, Special Collections & Archives.

title: The Human Condition: An Exploration of Art & Literature | Exhibit
description: The Human Condition: An Exploration of Art & Literature is an annual art and literary magazine created by medical students for the UC San Diego School of Medicine community. Now in its 32nd year, the student-led publication features art, photography, poetry, prose, sculpture, comics and more, providing a space for safe expression, creativity and exploring identities beyond medicine. This exhibition presents selected works from the 2025 and 2026 issues, offering a glimpse into the experiences, perspectives and creative lives of the School of Medicine community. Visitors are invited to pause, reflect and explore the many dimensions of the human experience. The Human Condition: An Exploration of Art & Literature is on view in the Sally T. WongAvery Library breezeway from September 26 to December 13, 2026, during the building's open hours. Previous issues of The Human Condition magazine, dating back to 2007-08, are available to download and read at your leisure. Curated by: Amy Xue, MS4, editor-in-chief, 2026-27 Myat Wai, MS4, editor-in-chief, 2026-27Supported by: UC San Diego School of MedicineUC San Diego Library

title: Library Milestones | Exhibit
description: Before the rise of digital publications and licensed electronic resources, academic libraries measured the size of their collections by the number of physical volumes on their shelves. Reaching a million-volume milestone was a source of pride and a mark of growth. This exhibit highlights five titles that mark milestones in the growth of the UC San Diego Library’s physical collections. Together, they also reflect the generosity of donors and support groups who helped build the collections and offer a glimpse into what made a book milestone-worthy at the time. Library Milestones is on view outside of Special Collections & Archives on the 2nd (main) Floor of Geisel Library during the building's open hours through Sunday, December 13, 2026. Photo citation: John Ogilby. America: being the latest, and most accurate description of the New World; containing the original inhabitants, and the remarkable voyages thither... London: printed by the author, 1671. UC San Diego Library, Special Collections & Archives.

title: More Than Pink Walk
description: The MORE THAN PINK Walk, Susan G. Komen’s largest fundraising event series, evolved from the Race for the Cure in 2018. Each year, we host over 100,000 participants at our 40+ in-person (and one virtual) walks across the U.S. Since the first Walk in 2018, our participants have raised more than $60 million dollars and continue to be a part of a community committed to our vision of a world without breast cancer. With inclusive and accessible options for people of all ages and abilities – including breast cancer survivors, those currently in treatment for breast cancer and people living with metastatic breast cancer – the Walk provides participants the opportunity to come together and connect in meaningful ways. It allows us to focus on sharing our passion, sharing our stories and connecting with others, all while fundraising to support life-saving programs and research. Our finish line is a world without breast cancer, and we know the only way we can get there is together.

description: Sensory-Friendly Quiet Mornings at the Museum The Museum’s sensory-friendly quiet hours are held every Sunday from 10 a.m. to 11 a.m. This time is dedicated to creating a calmer, quieter museum experience. We remain open to the public during this time, and all are welcome to visit the Museum. During this time, specific exhibit features in the main Museum building will be turned off to minimize audio and visual stimulation. Noise-blocking headphones are free for check-out at the main Admissions desk and the entrance to the Cannibals: Myth & Reality exhibition, Exhibit features in the Cannibals: Myth & Reality exhibit will remain on, and all exhibits will be fully turned on at 11 a.m. Admission purchased during sensory-friendly quiet hours is the same as standard admission and applies to the entire day. Please contact publicprograms@museumofus.org with any questions.

description: Visitors are welcomed onto our campus to attend our fun and festive AXIS events which are designed for the whole family. AXIS is a free, outdoor, multi-generational program that celebrates the cultural diversity of San Diego by inviting local artists and craftspeople to share their cultural traditions and heritage on the Globe’s Copley Plaza. Performances feature, dance, music, workshops, crafts and so much more.

title: Día de los Muertos at SDMA
description: Come together with family, friends, and the community at large at a special, free community event celebrating and honoring Día de los Muertos. Enjoy live performances, family-friendly art-making activities, and a special Día de los Muertos ofrenda created by visiting artist Betsabeé Romero in collaboration with local San Diego students, all in the Balboa Park Plaza de Panama in front of The San Diego Museum of Art and free to the community. Through artist-designed artmaking activities, community members will be invited to honor loved ones, share memories, and contribute meaningful objects and creative responses to the ofrenda on view in the plaza. Romero will join the Museum community for the inauguration of the SDMA ofrenda on Sunday, November 1 at 11:00 a.m. on the Museum’s front steps. The Taco Party , a gathering featuring unlimited street-style tacos, refreshing beverages, music, and a festive atmosphere, is a ticketed event complementing Día de los Muertos at SDMA. Free admission to The San Diego Museum of Art (SDMA) and the Museum of Photographic Arts at The San Diego Museum of Art (MOPA@SDMA) on Sunday, November 1 at noon–5:00 p.m. further complements the Día de los Muertos celebration.

title: The Taco Party
description: Join us for The Taco Party, a lively gathering featuring unlimited street-style tacos, refreshing beverages, music, and a festive atmosphere, all in the Museum’s sculpture court and garden. Designed as a fun and welcoming celebration for all ages, The Taco Party brings together great food, community, and the joyful spirit of Día de los Muertos. The Taco Party is part of Día de los Muertos at SDMA , a day of community highlighting a special ofrenda created by the community and designed by this season’s Visiting Artist Betsabeé Romero, transforming the Museum into a powerful tribute to remembrance and celebration. The Taco Party is a special ticketed portion of the Día de los Muertos celebration bringing together great food, community, and the joyful spirit of the holiday. The Taco Party is designed as a fun and welcoming celebration for all ages. title: Shaping a Library | Exhibition
description: In early 1970, a San Diego newspaper announced, “Unique Library Taking Shape.” The headline referred to UC San Diego’s Central University Library, now Geisel Library, which was then under construction. The Library’s story began several years earlier. In 1965, architect William L. Pereira was invited to design the Central University Library, envisioned as the flagship building for the UC San Diego campus. Construction began in 1968, and by September 1971, the new Central University Library was dedicated. Over the decades, the building has continued to evolve through expansions and renovations, adapting to the changing needs of the campus community. Tracing the history of the Library’s site design process, construction and expansion from 1965 to 1993, Shaping a Library draws on unique materials from UC San Diego Library’s Special Collections & Archives. From Pereira’s original spherical concept for Geisel Library to Gunnar Birkerts’ glass-walled expansion, architectural drawings, photographs and documents reveal the ideas, people and processes that shaped this beloved campus landmark. Shaping a Library is on view in the Exhibition Gallery on the 2nd (main) Floor of Geisel Library during the building's open hours from Saturday, September 26 through Tuesday, December 8, 2026. Can’t make it to campus to view the exhibition in-person? View the digital exhibit. Image Credit: Architectural rendering of UC San Diego Central University Library, William L. Pereira and Associates, 1965. UC San Diego Library, Special Collections & Archives.

Now in its 32nd year, the student-led publication features art, photography, poetry, prose, sculpture, comics and more, providing a space for safe expression, creativity and exploring identities beyond medicine. This exhibition presents selected works from the 2025 and 2026 issues, offering a glimpse into the experiences, perspectives and creative lives of the School of Medicine community. Visitors are invited to pause, reflect and explore the many dimensions of the human experience. The Human Condition: An Exploration of Art & Literature is on view in the Sally T. WongAvery Library breezeway from September 26 to December 13, 2026, during the building's open hours. Previous issues of The Human Condition magazine, dating back to 2007-08, are available to download and read at your leisure. Curated by: Amy Xue, MS4, editor-in-chief, 2026-27 Myat Wai, MS4, editor-in-chief, 2026-27Supported by: UC San Diego School of MedicineUC San Diego Library

title: Library Milestones | Exhibit

title: Supervising at UC San Diego - Nov. 3 & Nov. 10
description: Two day offering occurs Nov. 3 and Nov. 10, 9 a.m.-12 p.m. PST This orientation provides an overview of the most important do’s and don'ts of supervising at UC San Diego, emphasizing an approach where supervisors/managers are grounded in best practices, recognize areas that may implicate laws and regulations, and connect with resources to help navigate supervisory challenges. Additionally, this course provides an introduction to the employee life cycle and identifies managerial responsibilities, as well as applicable tools and resources at each stage.
